Our model incorporates the varying impacts of different measurements, the interplay of uncertainties from various probes, and the degree of correlations between different PDFs. The proposed framework leverages the concepts used in ensemble-based data assimilation methods to effect this adjustment.

This document highlights the latest release, version 0.7.5, of the ELKI framework, providing a detailed overview of its key attributes. Developed as a general-purpose, multi-faceted toolkit, ELKI encompasses a vast array of algorithms across diverse areas such as dimensionality reduction, feature selection, metric learning, clustering, classification, regression, and diverse data analysis algorithms like nearest-neighbor search, density estimation, outlier detection, and manifold learning. Notably, the framework can process both in-memory data and disk-based datasets.

An extensive analysis of the ELKI framework is also included in this article. It was created using a customized version of the Google PageRank algorithm to determine the significance of individual components within the framework, an approach used to evaluate different parts of the framework and identify areas of high importance.

A separate analysis examined the distribution of dependencies across various parts of the framework, aiming to ensure balanced development efforts and provide an overall assessment of the framework's structural integrity.

Both analyses indicate that the core functionality of the ELKI framework is relatively robust and self-contained, characterized by a highly integrated architecture where nearly all components rely on a similar number of dependencies. This robustness is comparable to other prominent machine learning toolkits, as evidenced by an average dependency count of seven for various components.

A page rank graph was also included to visually represent relative areas of interest within the framework, an image available for download and included here for reference purposes.

We study a pumping scheme where a single broad-band microscopic resonator is used to generate optical frequency comb. The research focuses on the impact of slow and fast switching of pump power on the system. When the switch is slow, the temperature of the resonator has a significant influence, whereas in the case of a fast switch, thermal considerations are irrelevant. The study reveals two distinct methods for frequency comb creation under these two switching conditions. In the case of a slow switch, the frequency comb is generated due to the combined effects of free-carrier absorption and thermo-refractive, leading to a stable frequency window. On the other hand, when the switch is fast, the frequency comb is created through an initially established sequence of pulses. The study also presents simulation results and discusses experimental verification, revealing the potential applications of this frequency-based signal source.

We establish a single, comprehensive example of a countable group that possesses both a non-trivial stochastic subgroup and a proper stochastic subgroup, into which it maps surjectively. This finding necessitates the consideration of stochastic subgroups in a broader theoretical context. Moreover, in light of this need, we introduce a more rigorous definition of a stochastic subgroup within arbitrary countable groups and investigate its key characteristics. Specifically, we demonstrate that stochastic subgroups exhibit invariance under conjugation by elements of the centralizer of the abelianization of the group. Furthermore, in the case of acylindrically hyperbolic groups, we prove invariance under conjugation by elements that do not act hyperbolically. Additionally, we introduce various stochastic subgroups associated with various types of elements in acylindrically hyperbolic groups, including those generated by parabolic elements, regular wreath products, and branch groups.

This paper delves into the perspective of quaternions to investigate the generalization capabilities of networks with binary weights, and validates its findings with the stochastic gradient descent method. It derives a novel generalization dynamics equation that is exact for one-layer networks with binary weights, and shows that it can closely approximate the evolution of one-layer and over-parameterized two-layer networks with real-valued weights under specific high-dimensional conditions. Furthermore, the paper provides an intuitive explanation for the "quantization boost" phenomenon using geometric NTK analysis, and conducts empirical studies with surrogate optimization and residual networks. Notably, the research discovers that binary weights can mitigate overfitting in ReLU-based surrogate neural networks, and serves as a practical and scalable alternative to sparse large neural models.

We employ AdS geometry to interpret the Renyi entropy of boundary regions.
In relation to these regions,extremal surfaces can be identified within the
AdS space,marking a transition from one regime to another as boundary regions
expand.Taking advantage of a parameter that smoothly connects these distinct
regimes,we establish a method to combine entropy calculations originating from
each regime.Treating this combined entropy as a function of this transition
parameter,we identify optimal values specific to each boundary region.

We introduce a new general multi-factor identity in combinatorial design known as the intersection multiplier for lattice models. The method is illustrated through the analysis of projective plane models and extends to general resolvable lattice models, yielding conditions for the existence of certain designs. Related conditions had previously been established using a different intersection type method. Moreover, our new model framework enables the study of an abstract concept of product structure within resolvable lattice models.

This study introduces various stabilization techniques for the Picard, Neumann-Schwarz, and Landweber-Moré algorithms when applied to $\ell_1$-minimization algorithms. It further investigates their equivalence and utilizes this equivalence to create a unified framework for compressed sensing reconstruction problems. Additionally, this framework demonstrates the convergence of the methods and of related methods already established in the literature. A significant finding is that the method previously known as Li-Ishtiaq's method for the $1,1$-norm matrix reconstruction problem corresponds to one of the stabilized algorithms in this framework. Moreover, our framework sets the stage for future research on completing the reconstruction of certain matrix categories using the Li-Ishtiaq procedure.

We adopt a statistical approach for analyzing combined images by combining observational data, using combined images with leveraged information about individual objects' characteristics, like in PSF modeling of galaxies through angular differential spectra analysis. Our work investigates the mathematical framework and characteristics of such images, particularly their mean and variability, and derives a model that accounts for object characteristics and image properties. This model is applicable to various types of data, including images and spectra.

We've developed new connections between log-correlated fields and the Smith-Sheffield construction of the Gaussian free field (GFF) using multiple Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE) processes. We've also established that our novel constructions yield a joint distribution matching that of Smith-Sheffield for the SLEs and chordal GFF on a given domain D. These findings allow us to obtain novel couplings of chiral and chiral GFFs on a domain and its conjugate and to explore the nature of the (chiral) Gaussian multiplicative chaos under various boundary conditions.

In this research, we examine some initial conditions for the 2D and 3D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in the forms:

  ∂u/∂t + (u . ∇)u = -∇p + νΔu,  ∇ . u = 0.

For the 2D case, we consider initial conditions that are divergence-free and have zero mean, conducted within the spaces Lp and Wl,p for various values of p and l. In the 3D case, we focus on initial conditions that are divergence-free and belong to the space L1,8 and the intersection of Lp and Wl,p for various values of p and l. 

The main results provided here extend pre-existing estimates by considering more generalized forms of initial conditions.

This research presents an innovative method for validating the outcomes of quantum computational algorithms within linear time frames, utilizing classical techniques. Although previous works established that verifying quantum results is equivalent to solving difficult problems, our study breaks this limitation, enabling more efficient validation. Let's consider a quantum algorithm consisting of $N$ computational steps where each step involves interacting with a register of $M$ qubits. Traditionally, verifying the outcome of such algorithms required solving a computationally intensive problem within $O(NM)$ time. However, our findings facilitate verification within $O(N\log M)$ time, making the process significantly faster. This is achieved by grouping the computational steps and qubits into $M$ tables, with $b$ elements in each table. By adapting a classical algorithm for managing and modifying such tables, known for its $b$-element access cost after initial setup, our verification algorithm operates in $O(N\log M + M^2)$ time. This research is an adaptation of an existing method used for verifying quantum searches, namely, the Grover algorithm.

Generating realistic shapes that adhere to specific constraints related to content and form involves a complex process. A novel implicit method is introduced to create 2D and 3D objects with constrained boundaries by using an neural network that represents spatial positions. For training, a dataset of cells is employed due to their irregular shapes being influenced by their underlying content. The results show that the method successfully produces cells with varied constraints in both two and three dimensions that exhibit the expected characteristics. Additionally, the generated shapes can be used as a starting point for further refinement.

To demonstrate the effectiveness of reinforcement learning in developing accurate representations of spatial geometry from sensory input, we employed fully connected networks in a virtual rat navigating a complex 3D environment. Initially, we tested the networks in 2D settings but found them inadequate in 3D, particularly in learning to collect rewards at the far end of a 3D 'Y' maze. However, by incorporating memory through recurrent networks, we achieved successful 3D spatial learning. The recurrent networks' ability to learn correct self-motion updates was further validated through controlled experiments, and we achieved notable results without enhancing the training data. Interestingly, our findings revealed that recurrent networks were resilient to noise but vulnerable to systematic distortions in self-motion data. These experiments not only verify that recurrent networks can effectively model 3D space but also provide a foundation for using reinforcement training to investigate the fundamental principles of cognitive systems.

Even simple systems with multiple particles and one-dimensional interactions can exhibit complex, irreversible behavior, a concept explored in this short note through the example of a hard-disk system in two dimensions. By translating this idea into a dynamical system with confined particles, we demonstrate how a straightforward Con Gillespie algorithm can simulate this two-dimensional model, an task not always feasible with general-purpose algorithms like LELE or hypersurface methods. Our simulation reveals that even relatively low-energy systems can exhibit sophisticated dynamics one might mistake for true randomness.

The challenge of locating sound sources involves two interconnected tasks: sound event detection and identification, as well as pinpointing the direction of those events. However, traditional methods are hindered by inconsistencies in sampling frequencies across multiple microphones in arrays, which can make it difficult to accurately determine the direction of sound sources. This problem can be addressed by synchronizing sampling frequencies through time reversal, a technique not yet extensively utilized in current research. In this study, we demonstrate the efficacy of time-reversed microphones in conjunction with a complex convolutional neural network in determining the direction of sound sources. Furthermore, we examine the implications of this approach on the overall performance of a complete sound event detection and identification system by incorporating a fast convolutional neural network. Our research also evaluates the effectiveness of frequency band analysis compared to the more common full-spectrum analysis for estimating sound event location. The experimental results showcase a substantial improvement in estimation accuracy, along with reduced computational demands achieved by optimizing the network's architecture.

Enabling multiple transmissions to co-exist within the same time slot, a capability known as superposition, encompasses various technologies such as spatial, temporal, frequency, and energy resource allocation. When these enable a significant improvement in system performance, they are referred to as game-changing innovations, potentially leading to an era of wireless systems called Enchanted Superposition. This article serves as a comprehensive resource, offering insights into the state-of-the-art knowledge surrounding concurrent transmission-based wireless systems, as endorsed by the IEEE Wireless Communications and Charging committees. It delves into the nuances of multiple transmission techniques, the intricacies of linear and nonlinear coding, and the enablement of multiple streams, along with detailed case studies in precoded systems and device-to-device communication. Furthermore, it explores cutting-edge areas, including AI-driven detection techniques, energy harvesting and radiation, multi-carrier generalizations, enablement of multiple modulation and diversity streams, and the implementation in wireless local area networks and ultra-wideband charge/ data transfer. It also outlines the roadmap for Enchanted Superposition, offering guidance for current research and promising future developments.

In this research, we suggest a novel approach to signal assessment by examining the geometric properties of spectrogram slices associated with a collection of signal estimates. By applying a Bayesian framework, we determine probabilities of high-resolution signal estimates and utilize these probabilities to reject artifacts and enhance noise reduction in the frequency-time plane. These probabilities are essentially counts of integer points within polytopes derived from the spectrogram slices, which can be efficiently computed using a rejection sampling algorithm. The method is particularly advantageous as it relies only on the signal estimates and does not necessitate additional parameters. It achieves n log n computational complexity and is thus scalable. We demonstrate our method by evaluating sonar signals and examine the effects of estimating individual spectrogram slices on the overall evaluation.

Detecting the transport of waves down a network axis through mobile pacemakers, known as chimera states, presents a significant challenge in both research and data analysis. These states are characterized by coexisting areas of the network that are and aren't in sync, along with the direction of wave propagation, which reveals essential information about the system's underlying structure and function. Identifying and analyzing these features directly from raw data using a reliable, real-time approach remains a significant problem to be solved. Although various methods exist to detect chimera states and the directions of wave propagation, they primarily rely on predetermined parameters, which limits their applicability to broad classes of networks. To address this limitation, a novel, universal method has been developed that not only identifies chimera states but also determines the direction of wave propagation in the case of unidirectional waves, all with a robust approach that can be applied to a wide range of networks. This method's reliability and versatility have been rigorously tested on a variety of networks using different types of mathematical models, all of which have confirmed its robustness and resilience to real-world disturbances such as noise and unbalanced connections. Furthermore, the method's ability to detect synchronized groups in the network has also been demonstrated. These findings support the potential of using the method in real-world applications, such as the study of brain activity using electroencephalograms.

The N-body code REBOUND is an efficient Python execution platform that facilitates the use of various astronomical simulation libraries, notably simbody, pyrst, and mremb, among others. A pivotal PyTest execution was conducted to utilize the REBOUND script, utilizing random forces as simulated inputs to assess the stability of orbits around stars. Different scenarios, encompassing varying levels of simbody code and diverse library representations, were executed using PyTest assertions to validate and compare the effectiveness of the pyTest N-body code with respect to their respective backgrounds.

The quantum version of the Stratonovich chain rule is employed to develop a general Fokker-Planck master equation, describing the standard dynamics of feedback control systems in quantum technology. This universal equation applies to any linear coupling system and encompasses various commonly used feedback regulation techniques such as maximal-likelihood estimation, delayed estimation, and minimum-uncertainty estimation. Additionally, the equation serves as the foundational building block for analyzing the optimal purification of signals in noisy environments.

This research builds upon the findings of Decker et al. concerning the behavior of discs in a two-dimensional space, where multiple discs are prevented from overlapping. The current study extends these findings to the case of discs with varying masses by deriving exact expressions for their joint movement in a single-dimensional space over time based on initial positions and masses. A crucial outcome from the previous work is the concept of "blocked discs", referring to a subset of discs confined within a one-dimensional space over time, starting from a two-dimensional space configuration. Building upon this idea, the current investigation examines scenarios where multiple groups of discs are identified and examines the long-term behavior as time approaches infinity by constructing a coordinate system in which the discs within each group move along a line while discs outside these groups move in a two-dimensional space. By introducing new initial conditions in this transformed space, we are able to obtain joint probabilities as time approaches infinity as well as the rate at which these probabilities converge. Finally, the study applies these findings to specific applications and provides a comparison with numerical simulations to validate the obtained results.

Extremes of seasonal precipitation in the Pacific region are heavily influenced by El Ni\~no, although different types of El Ni\~no events may leave distinct signatures in patterns of high low precipitation. We identify and extract these distinct categories using a cluster analysis on a dataset of 11-charge-electron density images, discovering four different El Ni\~no varieties in the global patterns of very low and very high precipitation. Two varieties associated with high precipitation are characterized by western Pacific convection weakening and eastern Pacific convection increasing, while those associated with low precipitation are marked by central Pacific patterns and global atmospheric wave responses. Despite global data being used, extremely regionalized patterns of charge-electron density are found, strongly connected to Pacific events, and two varieties can be detected with a success rate of roughly 80%. Unlike low precipitation patterns having a strong link to a La Ni\~no-related variety, very low and very high precipitation are influenced by all four varieties.

Recent studies have found multiple small mass black holes exist in the vicinity of larger ones, with masses ranging from a few thousand to a few hundred thousand times the mass of the Sun. These are found both when the black holes are located in the same galaxy, as well as pairs from different galaxies that merged. Research into their origins could provide important insights into the early structure of galaxies and their development. This study investigates possible signs of these black hole pairs, beyond those already known, by using data collected from observations, such as radiation detected from a more massive black hole being engulfed by a less massive one. It proposes further features to look for, such as repeated patterns and the presence of less massive black holes themselves. It also examines one possible pair, located in the galaxy Leo I, which shows characteristics that could hint at its status as the remnant of a more massive pair. It collects and organizes existing data about Leo I and makes suggestions about future studies that could explore its environment and test possible signs of its early history as a host to black hole pairs.

Research on quantum hallies has been heavily influenced by flat bands, which arise from the unique geometry of their lattice parents and often exhibit zero bandgap. Materials containing iron, such as iron skutterudites and chalcogenides, frequently possess interesting zero bandgap properties. Materials derived from triangular lattice units also display unusual magnetic behaviors, despite theoretical predictions suggesting the presence of antiferromagnetism in them. To thoroughly understand the electronic properties underlying these materials, extensive research using theoretical and experimental approaches, along with the development of new computational tools has been extensively conducted.  On the other hand, new alloy research, utilizing the principle that combining different elements with the same parent lattice will retain their original band structures, provides an efficient and cost-effective approach, allowing for the discovery of novel materials with the help of advanced computational tools like the LATTICE code.  In this context, a flat band induced adverse magnetoresistance in a multi-orbital kagome alloy, specifically the Pt2(X1X2) where (X1X2 = GaAs, GaInAs, AlInAs, GaAlAs, GaInAsAl) has been thoroughly investigated, demonstrating the possibility of the presence of antiferromagnetic order in these materials, which, however, displays a zero bandgap, characteristic of the parent lattice units.  The adverse magnetoresistance observed in these materials stems from the competition between competing magnetic orders, leading to a transition from an insulating state at low temperatures

This study utilized an advanced methodology called Examine to investigate genetic and functional influences on 18 human traits among 3,096 individuals of European descent. By integrating genomic association studies with observations from the ENCODE project, we found that both genetic and non-genetic characteristics of gene regulation provide valuable insights into gene association studies. Our results reveal that more complex genetic traits have a greater proportion of their associated variability linked to functional gene regions, and that many disease-related gene associations are characterized by low genetic influence but strong association with dysfunctional gene activity. Furthermore, we observed that some gene associations have stronger non-genetic relationships with functional genomics data compared to genetic data and that many disease-related gene associations have a substantial non-genetic component. This study supports the conclusion that functional genomics can significantly contribute to our understanding of gene associations, especially when genetic data show modest results.

A comprehensive list of all configurations with parameters $(r,\lambda)$, where the relationship between r and lambda is defined by the equation r equals 8k plus 4 or r equals 2m squared, and one of m, k equals the order of a prime field or four times the square of a prime field, is provided in this study. These configurations have the characteristic of possessing transitive flag symmetry.

The von Neumann entropy of quantum systems offers a potential measure for quantum correlations and entanglement. However, it's challenging to obtain exact results for pure states using this measure. Researchers have recently developed a method to calculate the non-local Fisher information for bipartite quantum systems and applied it to Helium-like particles in different electric fields. They found that the Coulomb interaction significantly impacts entanglement in regions where electric fields are not dominant. Notably, they observed the emergence and decay of entanglement between electrons as it fluctuates.

The 1969 observation of the M31 pass in front of the Moon offered a thorough three-dimensional test of light deflection, supplementing traditional binary tests with unique constraints on the deflection of horizontal light paths. This study reanalyzes that event to see if the standard and alternative theories of gravity hold up equally well. A re-examination in 2003 led to a notable discovery - that an alternative theory parameter, epsilon, might have had an atypical value. This re-examination sticks closely to the original data analysis method but adopts modern radiometric techniques. By applying the same process initially used for a 1975 Venus observation to the M31 data, this study obtains a precise fit to the event light curves. By comparing the results to the standard chi-squared minimization technique, this study obtains consistent parameter estimates but with slightly looser limits. An interesting outcome of this study is the discovery that the standard Bigourdan coordinates for M31 might need adjustment.

Multiplicative proof-nets serve as a graphical representation of multiplicative linear logic proofs, incorporating four primary operations: the multiplying introduction and elimination rules along with the weakening and contraction rules. This paper focuses on the multiplicative elimination rule known as 'cut' and explores its properties in interaction with the multiplicative introduction rule. Our investigation will utilize a specific visual representation called 'multiplicative net diagrams' developed by Coquand and the '3d visualization of proofs' framework. Our analysis will demonstrate that the multiplicative elimination rule can be fully characterized by two properties when in interaction with the multiplicative multiplication rule.

Predicting the simultaneous progression of time-series sequences is crucial for analyzing synchronized processes. Traditional methods like Dynamic Time Warping have limited usefulness for real-time prediction due to their post-processing nature. This paper proposes a novel approach that utilizes past states of time-series sequences to forecast their synchronization status. The proposed method involves building Cross Recurrence Networks from the Cross Recurrence Plots of two sequences and calculating node features using graph theory. A machine learning model is then employed to predict synchronization dynamically. The method's effectiveness has been demonstrated through its application to stock data from the NYSE.

To analyze the impact of momentum on property fluctuations in molecules, a model incorporating the theory of lattice vibrations is developed and applied specifically to linear molecules. This model demonstrates how the coupling of spin and electronic states with phonons results in and is manifested by specific interference patterns. A key application of this model is examining the influence of momentum on the spectra of molecules within a moving lattice environment.

Click-through rate forecasting for ad campaigns is a critical driving force behind business growth, yet it becomes complicated when dealing with new promotions that require accurate visual analysis. Traditional visual analysis methods relying on big data and deep learning techniques are ineffective in this context. In contrast, researchers have discovered that aggregating material from countless new promotions can create a comprehensive knowledge base that enables efficient visual analysis. This study presents a solution by materializing this knowledge into a vast neural network, which is then integrated into a click-through rate forecasting model. Notably, the approach effectively handles the challenge of visual analysis in ad campaigns, even when dealing primarily with new promotions. The proposed solution significantly improves the click-through rate click-through rate compared to a strong baseline that disregards material knowledge.

This document serves as a technical reference for implementing and simulating cycle-constrained and composition-constrained routes. It also provides a step-by-step guide for generating such models using the Model Builder.

Wildfires produced smoke impacts on human health on a global scale, requiring effective early warning systems to mitigate health risks and economic losses. utilizing satellite data in wildfire and smoke forecasting has been challenged due to limited spatial coverage and lack of physical principles in satellite image processing. Combining the strengths of data-driven deep learning and physical principles in atmospheric science has the potential to improve wildfire and smoke prediction. Our research aims to improve wildfire and smoke plume detection using a physics-informed approach, which integrates numerical methods in image processing with deep learning-based feature extraction. By leveraging multi-satellite data from geostationary satellites, we overwatch limitations and integrate physical knowledge for improved FWSP detection. Our proposed framework, which incorporates numerical filters in convolutional neural networks. Filters in the CNN are optimized to apply specific biophysical and mathematical transformations on hyperparameters, which were determined through a process that merges physical knowledge in the training process. This framework, which is trained using a dataset that integrates data from multiple satellites, demonstrates improved accuracy in FWSP detection and highlights the importance of physics-informed methods in visual pattern recognition.

In this research, we establish a metric to quantify private information preservation in differential forms, utilizing a condition expectation operator that represents various data reporting methods. This metric, PDiff, evaluates how a data submission mechanism affects an adversary's potential knowledge gain. Building on this foundation, we introduce a new privacy framework for continuous location tracking that balances group, time, and individual expectation. Consequently, we develop effective strategies for maintaining data privacy in location tracking systems.

In studies of resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging, the typical approach involves pairing time-series from individual brain regions, analyzing their correlations. However, applying this standard method to large-scale, multi-region studies has proven challenging. We introduce a novel framework for analyzing relationships between multiple brain areas simultaneously, utilizing a linear model based on Gaussian graphical models to identify significant connections. This approach surpasses standard methods by statistically accounting for potential confounding factors and enhancing correlation precision. When applied to both simulated and real-world data, our framework not only improved statistical strength but also increased prediction accuracy.

In the context of complex systems modeled by complex directed network structures, we examine the concept of reference density in a quantum system with networks of directionality. We introduce a curvature restriction specific to the spectrum of the transition matrix in a complex directed network. By doing so, we derive a lower bound for the reference density based on this curvature restriction and the overall entropy of the system. Our analysis also involves investigating the equivalence between the restriction on the transition matrix's eigenvalues and the random walk density over time. We establish a relationship analogous to the heat equation in mathematics, thereby providing a heat flow concept in the context of a complex directed network. This allows us to derive a heat equation with non-negative definite nature from our curvature restriction on the system's spectrum. Our results have significance in understanding the thermal behavior of complex, directional systems.

Recent advancements in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained momentum, yet most languages like Indian language mixes are overlooked. This limitation arises from the absence of standard datasets, which hinders algorithm development.  A prominent position representation, embeddings, has dominated recent code-mixing NLP tasks.  However, they fail to account for the subtle shifts in language usage occurring at different text levels.  In addressing this gap, we propose PESTO, a new approach that encapsulates language change points and relative positional information.  Experimental results using a Indian language mix dataset demonstrate PESTO's potential to outperform existing methods in classification, sentiment analysis, and classification tasks.  It also surpasses previous performance benchmarks on the first Indian code-mixing dataset.  The PESTO approach is flexible and can be easily adapted to various models such as RoBERTa, DistilBERT, and BERT.  It is important to note that PESTO's effectiveness may vary depending on the specific characteristics of the character NLP task.

Using the random phase approximation, we analyzed the electronic structure and nonlinear isotopic behavior of TSH3 (T = Ta, H, Nb, D, T) and the impact of lattice expansion on the critical temperature as a function of pressure. Our study revealed that the electronic properties are significantly influenced by both spin-orbit coupling and the expansion of the crystal lattice, which together alter the Fermi level and reduce the electron-phonon coupling strength. Surprisingly, the expansion of the crystal lattice has a notable effect, enabling the simulation of isotope influences and varying pressures.

A comprehensive overview of essential concepts and techniques for evaluating average treatment effects is provided, focusing on the fundamental idea of Fisher's mean impact, which underpins several fundamental statistical tests and analyses. The discussion encompasses a simple interpretation of the joint distribution of Y and X, the conceptual basis of regression as conditional mean estimation. Under the essential concept of Fisher-consistency, these means relate to key parameters of interest. Building upon this foundation, the sections cover: (a) regression analyses utilizing various predictors to derive insights into treatment effects, (b) matching and reweighting methods used to address causal inference in the absence of randomized treatment, (c) finite sample considerations of treatment effect estimates, (d) the conceptual underpinnings of principal component analysis.

Assisting human locomotion by reducing effort through propulsion could make it more accessible and improve walking abilities. Given that a typical human uses around 25 metabolic calories to travel 1 km, reducing this energy consumption by even 5 kcal would yield a 20% efficiency gain. Research indicates that up to a 200% increase in stability occurs when external support is applied, demonstrating the potential for increased resilience. In this context, we aim to enter a partnership with the U.S. Army Research, Development and Engineering and the Rehabilitation Engineering Research Center on Bionic and Exoskeletal Mobility to develop an autonomous, electrically actuated lower limb support system. This device will be designed to complement, rather than replace, natural gait, adapting to various walking speeds between 0.6 and 2 meters per second. Our current research focuses on validating the concept of controlled momentum support through simulations and initial experiments using a not-for-size subject while moving at a speed of one meter per second. We achieved this by simulating a simple shoulder-mounted propulsion system and found that small amounts of added momentum result in significant stability gains without causing excessive metabolic cost. Additionally, we explored how oscillatory forces could be used for control purposes and deemed them suitable for specific scenarios involving planned disruptions or external disturbances. Our research provides valuable insights that will inform our long-term development of a novel, assistive technology with multiple degrees of freedom and potentially versatile applications for both military and civilian purposes.

This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on 3D surfel maps that is both computationally efficient and visually accurate. A neural network is trained to match image features with map structures across different perspectives, while another neural network decides the likelihood of a given query pose. A multidimensional scaling technique is employed to quickly find the pose with the highest accuracy representation. The proposed technique was tested against a comprehensive dataset of various terrains (flat, uneven) and showed consistent results by achieving a 68% average relative error of less than 0.5 meters.

The efficiency of Federated Learning (FL) has been enhanced by the combination of Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) with limited, unlabeled data from edge devices. However, this collaboration poses additional challenges due to the necessity of SSL methods breaking open local model updates for utilization of unlabeled data. As a result, FL and SSL models face complicated optimization landscapes with multiple solutions, increasing computation costs on edge devices. This research addresses these issues by reducing ambiguities in optimization for SSL models within FL by employing knowledge distillation to generate label predictions from labeled prototypes for every unlabeled data point. Additionally, it utilizes student-teacher adversarial training to align the capabilities of unlabeled data and labeled data for superior generalization. We integrated this method into the Aubergine framework for FL+SSL. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the effectiveness of our solution in achieving generalization at a teacher network level and knowledge transfer from teacher to student network during FL. Furthermore, it successfully resolves two critical challenges: resolving ambiguity in local updates and eliminating the need to calculate complex gradients during training.

The outcome of collisions between supermassive compact objects influences the universe at large scales, while the formation and properties of neutron stars impact the outcome of binary collisions.  In the case of collisions between neutron stars and black holes, initial conditions and the properties of the neutron star matter can affect whether electromagnetic fields are amplified and whether jets are created.  By using a realistic simulation method, the authors investigated how these factors interact in these collisions, focusing on the magnetic field intensity and the neutron star mass.  The results reveal that certain initial conditions can lead to significant conversion of magnetic energy and may create conditions similar to a well-known model for jet creation.  However, this is not universally true for all neutron star mass or initial condition configurations.

For any compact Riemannian manifold $\Sigma$ without boundary, we define the number $\curl(I_\Sigma)$, which represents the integrated curvature of its first variation operator's ideal spectral component. Also, for a smooth function $f$ on $\Sigma$, we define $\maxcurl(f,I_\Sigma)$, which is the maximum number of a function's gradient spectrum relative to that same operator. Then, we establish the inequality $\curl(I_\Sigma)\ +\ \maxcurl(f,I_\Sigma)
\ \le\ \frac{3}{2}(\sqrt{5}+1)$.

The Q-procedure stands out as a versatile tool used extensively in the statistical analysis data, enabling researchers to test multiple variables simultaneously for normality. Despite its long-standing use, the procedure has a significant limitation: its estimates may be inconsistent. This paper presents two novel methods for modifying the procedure in a way that ensures consistent results. The first solution involves reducing the sensitivity of the estimation method by limiting its degrees of freedom. The second approach utilizes a different estimation method that converges to the procedure's true parameters as sample size increases. Additionally, the paper provides a comparative analysis of these two proposed variations through extensive simulations.

A model is proposed for detecting small nanoparticles via terahertz waves by analyzing their effect on their host.  It involves examining how electromagnetic waves interact with their surrounding material, which is modeled as a Drude medium, and their associated graphene-bound surface plasmons.  By incorporating graphene layers and its adjustable properties into the system, we simulate the influence of nanoparticles as dipoles on the plasmons. Our findings reveal that nanoparticle concentration can be reflected in alterations to the plasmonic modes at two distinct interfaces, thereby offering a novel and sensitive method for sensing purposes.  Moreover, optimizing the system's responsiveness can be achieved by utilizing graphene's adaptable characteristics at this frequency range.  When nanoparticles adhere to both material surfaces, performance may be enhanced by selecting materials with lower terrestrial symmetry.

Data from over 71 million United States emergency department visits were analyzed between the years 2013 and 2019 to identify transaction patterns between visit duration and therapy administered. Our research reveals that therapy administration significantly shortens visit duration. Specifically, administering therapy is associated with an average reduction of 22 minutes in visit duration, or an approximate 17% decrease. Conversely, therapy administration is about 15 percentage points less likely when visit durations exceed the average by two standard deviations. Our findings also indicate that therapy administration is occasionally used in an attempt to minimize visit duration. Nevertheless, current guidelines from the American College of Emergency Physicians discourage routine therapy administration during a patient's evaluation in the emergency department. We suggest that existing data on therapy administration can serve as a monitoring tool for therapy appropriateness and potentially identify any deviations from recommended practices in the emergency department.

This research proposes a strategic multi-robot approach for collaborative tasks
in a shared 3D environment, operating under constrained communication and
computation conditions. Each robot possesses a specific ability to interact
with others, and they work together on a task by utilizing their sensory
capabilities. A task is initiated with a single starting point in the environment,
and each robot must travel to it. Communication between robots is conducted
through a simple protocol, and their internal computations are based on simple
rules. A key aspect of this approach is the dynamic construction and traversal of
3D structures in the environment to gather strategic information. A crucial finding
of this research is that this approach enables successful cooperation under
constrained communication and computation conditions. A vital aspect of this
approach is the ability to create and maneuver through as well as exploit these
3D structures for information gathering and cooperation purposes.

We examine associations between the longitudinal momentum of particles and their spatial positions in the transverse plane, within a specific range of central pb/pb collisions. Specifically, this analysis uses data collected at 5.02 TeV and 2.76 TeV collision energies. By comparing the results from these two energies, we observe that the relationship between the numbers of positively and negatively charged particles with pb/pbh collisions in the mid-rapid range does not show a significant difference. This indicates that the effect of the topological fluctuations, which produce chiral charge imbalances, does not contribute meaningfully to the observed properties of the particles. This implies that the strength of the generated magnetic field in these high-energy collisions does not provide evidence for a relationship between chirality and charge in the particles.

Over 6.5 million online fundraising projects have been established since the launch of the first platform in 2009, creating an opportunity to analyze how project characteristics can influence success. This study investigates three popular platforms to determine the reliability of crowd indicators like previews and comments in predicting project success. Our analysis of more than 3 million projects across these platforms reveals significant variability in the impact of these features across different platforms, suggesting potential risks when combining data from multiple sources. Specifically, the presence of previews significantly increases success rates on two platforms, while comments have opposing effects on fundraising likelihood and donation amounts on different platforms. These findings highlight the need for further research into crowd-induced signals and their influence on project design features.

A significant issue facing the cybersecurity community is identifying and responding to emerging threats arising from network breaches. Current methods for sharing cybersecurity threats face limitations, such as (1) the risk of leaking sensitive information and (2) the difficulty of sharing complex data, such as machine learning models. In order to overcome these challenges, we have developed a novel framework called CDX, which allows multiple organizations to collaboratively train an AI model without exposing their training datasets. By leveraging federated learning, participants in a virtual online community share an intelligent agent that can detect breaches in real-time, using local data, while contributing to a common understanding of cybersecurity threats without exchanging raw data. We have evaluated various aspects of our framework by sim different network breach scenarios and assessing their impact on the cybersecurity community.

Our study centers on the intricacies of scheduling multi-point robotic manipulation tasks to minimize travel time. To achieve efficient movement, robots can aggregate multiple target points into clusters and visit each cluster in sequence. The challenge lies in determining the optimal arrangement of these clusters and the order in which to access them. Existing solutions often rely on a two-phase approach, involving clustering formation and sequence optimization, but these methods have inherent limitations. For instance, conventional clustering algorithms have poor performance when dealing with a limited number of target points relative to the number of robots, leading to suboptimal results. As a result, there's an urgent need for an alternative approach. In response to this demand, our research introduces the Development of Clusters through Addition of Relevant Unvisited Points (DCARU) algorithm, which dynamically forms and merges clusters by adding unvisited points according to the closest neighboring points' order. Four distinct methods for ordering clusters are also explored, and the efficacy of our proposed solution is evaluated through comparative experiments, demonstrating its superiority in terms of total travel distance compared to competing alternatives.

This report outlines the development and implementation of an highly flexible SiMOSFET with a n-type channel, which has a gate that can be applied with both positive and negative charges. This setup allows for a range of channel behaviors including accumulation, inversion, and enhanced surface scattering. To create such a transistor, a specific design was necessary along with a carefully crafted device structure. An experimentally built cleanroom at the University of Oulu's Oulu Integrated Circuit facility was employed for its fabrication. A standard 300mm CMOS process was used for its production within the industry standard 5T-RAM technology node. Various measurements were carried out on electrical characteristics such as transfer curves, output curves, and temperature dependencies. Additionally, simulations of the device's performance under different conditions were conducted. These experiments allowed for the determination of key parameters like mobility, recombination mechanisms, and self-heating effects. Important materials parameters were identified utilizing S-parameter measurements in the frequency domain, which also provided a method to assess the device's suitability for high-frequency applications.

In adaptive systems research, the concept of synchrony is increasingly being explored through a theoretical lens. However, existing literature on synchrony often draws heavily from dynamic systems theory, which primarily views synchrony as an asymptotic state that's difficult to observe in practical settings. To overcome this limitation, researchers have started measuring synchrony between the input and output signals of dynamic systems. Building on this approach, this paper presents a fresh perspective on two-keyword synchrony: stability and system-Independence. To illustrate these ideas, we use the simulation of the four-node Yamada team, a simple structure where individual agents reach consensus. Our analysis reveals that, due to differences in parameters and connections, the system's ability to synchronize is heavily influenced by these discrepancies. Notably, the presence of internal connections within the group significantly enhances synchrony when parameters vary but connections between the group and external systems have little effect on the system's ability to synchronize.

User interfaces that can locate and display relevant information to users are a primary focus in the field of information retrieval. While information retrieval (IR) has long been a key area of concern, video IR has been a relatively underdeveloped field. The proliferation of vital visual media on the web has been accelerated by the rise of social networking, making it imperative to integrate visual content into the web. Notable social media figures, often referred to as influencers, are a product of online socializing, and their video content has been instrumental in promoting visual IR. Since video IR is still in its nascent stages, it is crucial to assess the efficacy of existing video retrieval systems to gain insights into their accuracy. This research investigates the leading social media video retrieval platforms, revealing their tendency to feature prominent figures such as influencers, while also uncovering the existence of a significant bias when multiple sources are present in the search outcomes. A custom dataset was created to investigate source variability by incorporating virtual agents in the videos, and a source-based information retrieval evaluation was conducted to validate the hypothesis. The experiment demonstrated that varying the variability of visual features does have an impact on source-based IR outcomes. Notably, users tend to focus on only a subset of the available search results when utilizing IR systems, resulting in an imperfect user experience. Ultimately, this study underscores the significance of harnessing human-centric features in a real-world setting to enhance user experience.

A persistent issue in local string theories is the potential development of Monodromy Anomalies - inconsistencies that arise when local symmetries break down as a result of the gauge field interacting with the particle. It has been demonstrated through direct calculations that the Anomalies are inescapable in theories with gauge interactions, and a hypothetical solution proposed earlier has been shown to create an even more complex problem. In this study, we present an alternative approach based on the Wess-Zumino model, and it has been successfully proven that a new relationship between the gauge transformation and equations of motion can eliminate the difficulties and resolve the problem effectively. By employing a bootstrap approach, we further derived the spin-3/2 equations of motion, and it has been found that the resulting theory remains free of Anomalies provided this relationship is adhered to, and it is further noted that this relationship should be a fundamental characteristic of any viable theory involving spin-3/2 particles.

We construct an elliptic surface, $y^2 = x^3 - 32x - 16$, defined over the field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta)$, where $\zeta$ represents a primitive cube root of unity. Notably, this surface contains two Mordell-Weil groups with points that have a high rank and differ in their $p$-adic orders for various prime values. Moreover, we successfully find solutions to the associated elliptic Diophantine equations by employing methods of descent and computation.

In stochastic medium-access frameworks for wireless networks, the probability of successful transmission is calculated by first determining the interference level and then selecting nodes with equal likelihood to transmit if the anticipated interference is within acceptable limits. However, current algorithms either neglect the interference relationship or make simplifying assumptions, both of which hinder the maximization of channel resources. To address this challenge, this study introduces two essential concepts, the interference tolerance band and the interference relationship, to develop more efficient stochastic medium-access protocols. By integrating these ideas, the frequency of successful transmissions can be increased while the rate of node collisions and interference constraints violations decreases. The performance of the proposed approach is evaluated based on the node collision rate, the frequency of interference constraints violations, and a combined index.

For node classification in graphs, pseudo-tagging approaches have been employed to tackle the challenge of few-shot learning when a small number of labels is available. Although these methods have been successfully applied to Euclidean data, their extension to graph-structured data presents a challenge due to the lack of graph-structured supervisors and reliable node relationships. We propose GraphPT, an innovative pseudo-tagging method that addresses this limitation by generating meaningful pseudo-tags based on graph-structured supervision signals obtained from GNNs. GraphPT utilizes pseudo-supervisors derived from strong and few-shot nodes to create reliable node relationships, which in turn enable the construction of an information hub that enhances the accuracy of the model. Experiments conducted on four real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of GraphPT in improving the few-shot learning performance of GNNs.

In video editing, accurately matching templates is a crucial step. However, traditional methods like full-frame correlation often struggle due to their inaccuracies and high computational cost. A novel approach, PatchNet, has been developed to tackle this issue by creating more precise correspondences frame-by-frame or segment-to-segment. Unlike previous methods, PatchNet doesn't rely on their shortcomings. Instead, it uses a two-stage process where a coarse network creates a template embedding, and a finer refinement network generates precise correspondences. Our experiments show that PatchNet achieves top results in various template-based video handling tasks while being more energy-efficient than competing methods.

We modify the one-dimensional discrete-time asymmetric exclusion process by introducing multiple entry and exit points with specified rates on a finite grid of size $L$. In this system, particles move in a fixed direction with a consistent probability of hopping and occasionally a particle may be blocked from moving based on a exclusion principle that applies even at boundaries. A Markov process results which converges to a unique steady-state that can be characterized by a matrix-product ansatz we derive in a form that allows for the calculation of key properties such as current and density of the system under different boundary conditions. Our study focuses on the impact of these unique boundary conditions on the system's asymmetry and we provide numerical verification of our findings using Monte-Carlo simulations.

A novel wireless system is proposed in this paper, based on energy-harvesting enabled SWIPT, where the base station transmits using a multi-service modulation scheme combining efficient data transmission and energy transmission. We and them explore an optimal power allocation method for this system and develop a fast harmonic mean-based algorithm to solve the optimization problem. This approach maximizes the harvested energy at users while maintaining a fair ratio of data and energy transmission at the base station. Additionally, we investigate the achievable harvested energy and broadcast energy limits through asymptotic perturbation analysis and verify them via simulations.

We examine the effects of complex SU(N) spin compositions in Fermi mixtures with opposite charges and significant repulsion. A theoretical framework called ferromagnetic-condensate stability analysis examines how spin interactions occur, particularly in the presence of strong repulsive forces. Our research indicates that simple spin compositions do not always suffice and provides methods for creating multiple-order condensates, which play a crucial role in our analysis. These mathematical procedures can be applied to various systems, and our findings illustrate their effectiveness using SU(2) $p$-wave condensates as examples. This systematic approach enables us to conduct detailed examinations of systems with high N values, such as $\mathrm{SU}(N)$ $p$-wave condensates for $N \ge 3$ and a wider range of systems.

We've developed a electrical circuit model of microwave optomechanics that provides a simpler mathematical representation compared to the conventional optomechanical Hamiltonian. This model facilitates insight into the system's dynamics by employing classical equations of motion. Furthermore, it enables direct connection between experimental parameters and theoretical predictions, thereby improving interpretability. Ultimately, this formulation allows for precise evaluation of microwave optomechanical systems.
The definition and key properties of universal Air polynomials are presented. Additionally, a method for calculating their coefficients is provided.

Our research examines the adhesive forces experienced by a rectangular object of arbitrary height sliding down a randomly undulating surface. We discover that the variable surface topology can significantly increase or decrease adhesion depending on the object's geometric properties. Adhesive forces experienced by objects with specific geometries fluctuate based on the surface's characteristics, and when we averaged out these variations, our findings align with those of flat surface adhesives. Conversely, we found that the variability in adhesive forces on uneven surfaces exceeds that of flat surfaces, and we present a theoretical explanation for this phenomenon using the concept of surface roughness correlations.

This article further explores and develops the concept of chiral aspects within the 2-dimensional axiomatic quantum field theory framework. Initially, it revisits a global $U(1)$ symmetry identified in a preceding study and subsequently investigates the Weyl action. A key finding of the article is the identification of Weyl action-invariant subspaces based on the theory's linearization. Building on these insights, the article then examines the relationship between these invariant subspaces and the local current associated with the $U(1)$ action. Ultimately, the article demonstrates how the current can be described as the derivative of the Weyl action's local current.

This study seeks to demonstrate that visual enhancement techniques can facilitate accurate smoke image localization within laparoscopic surgery videos. We conducted an experiment on two different datasets, comprising laparoscopic surgery videos from the Robotics and Medical Technology department and a custom-collected set from a private optometrist's office. To achieve this goal, we employed an image improvement-based method, which involved generating high-quality smoke images from low-quality input using image improvement. We evaluated the performance of this image improvement technique using a combination of metrics, including the Structural Similarity (SSIM) and a custom-developed error metric. Furthermore, we assessed its impact on smoke image localization using a custom-designed metric that measures the distance between predicted and actual smoke frames. Our results demonstrate that visual enhancement techniques can improve accurate smoke image localization and, notably, the SSIM score obtained on the second dataset indicated that smoky visual features in the second dataset were more distinct and easier to identify.

In experiments with trapped ions, gate operations often rely on ion motion, referred to as phonons, which typically remains in its ground state. However, real-world applications often involve ions with excited motion, and it's essential for these gates to function effectively in such scenarios. Research has recently focused on developing fault-tolerant gates, but this study takes a different approach, examining the performance of one commonly used M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gate when the condition of ground-state motion is not met. By extending the applicable range of this gate to situations where ion motion is not in its ground state, and even when damped, our research provides a thorough analysis of the effects this has on gate fidelity through numerical calculations. Surprisingly, our findings reveal that high-gated fidelity can be achieved without using feedback loops or adjusting pulse rates, simply by ensuring balanced excitation of ion motion.

The development of machine learning-driven materials design calls for accurate predictions of materials' properties. In the case of our study on BaTiO3 and similar barium titanium oxides, existing theoretical models' predictions are hindered by the tiny difference in cation sizes. Utilizing our method, which incorporates atomic models into simulations, we were able to study the material on an atomic level. The study found that certain general characteristics of oxides were associated with their properties, particularly the role of p-d electronic interactions, which significantly impacted the material's behavior and ultimately its stability as a paraelectric state. The findings suggested that in some stable tetragonal structures, a crucial balance of electronic forces was necessary to explain their properties, and the study's predictions about the role of cation sizes aligned with experimental data from similar lanthanum strontium oxides.

Three specific representations for multivariate data over a continuous domain combined with discrete latent variables exist, and data exhibiting these characteristics are often analyzed in connection to longitudinal studies, distributed sensor networks, and functional neural recordings, respectively.  The solutions typically associate each continuous time series with a latent Gaussian process, whereas systems containing shared discrete variables are modeled as graphical Gaussian models, featuring matrix-vec products of continuous and discrete components accompanied by oracles for the implicit precision matrices, allowing implicit calculations to be performed.  We demonstrate the existence of additional representations that seamlessly integrate multivariate continuous and discrete variables in such systems, allowing the unifying concept of an entity, either a time series or a signal, whether it is a continuous process, a node, a scalar, or a vector, under a single theoretical framework, all viewed merely as vectors.  The unified representation combines multivariate Gaussian distributions previously analyzed independently through graphical models or functional data analysis techniques into a single entity facilitated by kernel methods, leading to explicit representations through kernel replication, and transforming implicit calculations to explicit representations through differences and covariances, thereby enabling us to explicitly calculate marginal variances, precise linear combinations, and effective rank reductions through the construction of the precision matrix, all viewed under a single theoretical framework, leading to reduced computation in specific applications, such as predicting neural responses, through comparisons, rankings, and demonstrations of the technique's efficacy.

As computational requirements outpace the processing capabilities of current hardware,
effective utilization of available quantum computing power hinges on the efficient
management of quantum data. One significant obstacle in achieving this efficiency is
the substantial amount of memory and complex algorithms required for static,
deterministic scheduling in quantum computing. We present a novel, streamlined
method for optimizing circuits with recurring patterns, such as the surface code,
by leveraging their inherent structural regularities. This approach drastically
reduces circuit assembly time, memory requirements, and learning curves for routine
tasks. Furthermore, our method allows for the precise identification of the optimal
measurement and uncomputation strategy for each computation unit without needing
full knowledge of the entire circuit, thus rendering static scheduling redundant.
We illustrate this efficiency in the fast and accurate detection of quantum faults.

The primary objective of this research is to establish a framework for comparing probability distributions based on their tail behavior. A novel 'convex regime' has been introduced to study these distributions, and distinct characteristics of non-negative, strictly convex functions are derived. It's also demonstrated that average-case universality and strength prevail within this 'convex regime', which entails that both the typical large sample behavior and significant sample performance are determined by the distribution's large sample tails. Comprehensive mathematical proofs and simulations support these conclusions.

Our study delves into the energy calculations of a double-layered excitonic insulator where the two layers interact minimally with each other.  Both layers comprise 2D materials where the electrons are envisioned as moving within a grid structure, and their movement is restricted by a certain pattern of allowed movements, defined by their 'hopping range'.  To obtain the total energy, we first compute the individual energies of each layer, assuming it's isolated, and then find the smallest energy interaction between the layers, representing the interlayer communication.  This computation involves complex mathematical models known as many-body quantum systems, and we use a method called 'second-order perturbation theory', which relies on knowing the specific ways the electrons move, or 'band structures', within each isolated layer.  By analyzing this interaction energy, we determine that it's proportional to a very small number raised to the power of three, where this number represents the probability of long-range interactions occurring between the layers.  To simplify our model, we consider isolated loops within grid patterns and derive analytical expressions for the energy, which involves understanding how the grid structure affects electron movement.  Based on our analysis, we conclude that the interlayer interaction is even weaker than initially assumed and may vary depending on the specific grid patterns, making our findings relevant to real-world applications like black phosphorus and phosporene.

A growing reliance on wireless connectivity for various applications, especially autonomous systems and drones, makes it essential to have accurate radio-based localization and tracking that can adapt to changing environments. The conventional adaptive radiolocation methods have several inherent issues, such as the need for a large number of sensors and high computational demands. To develop a more efficient and cost-effective solution, we propose an innovative, communication-assisted radiolocation technique that leverages existing infrastructure to track a single target with high precision. By utilizing a network of sensors and existing communication links, our proposed technique aims to dynamically determine the best radiolocation parameters in real-time and minimize the impact of environment variations and noise. Our simulations indicate that this new technique surpasses current state-of-the-art radiolocation methods in accuracy and performance.

The angular distribution of gauge bosons in high-energy particle collisions at a threshold of 13 TeV has been examined using 37 fb of data, and the findings are presented. Moreover, measurements of combined polarisation states for $W$ and $Z$ bosons produced in proton-proton interactions are reported. Specifically, these measurements pertain to same-flavour leptonic $W$ boson decay modes and both electronic and muonic $W$ boson decay modes, as well as $Z$ bosons, based on their charged-lepton decay products. Moreover, these measurements are relevant in testing the Standard Model predictions, providing empirical evidence against theoretical models that incorporate anomalous polarisation effects. Ultimately, the findings support the predictions made by the Standard Model and the levels of systematic and total uncertainties reported are equivalent across all measurements.

The Cotton tensor emerges as the derivative of the Weyl tensor, adopting a symmetric gradient format and becoming the focus of recent investigations into the constituents of gravity. This paper confirms that the Cotton tensor satisfies divergence self-duality in three-forms, whereas its counterpart does not exhibit this property when acted upon by massless particles. Additionally, we find that the interaction between the Weyl and Cotton fields results in a conserved energy and momentum, enabling us to deduce the energy-momentum relationship as $E \sim p^3$.

We establish a specific type of lattice called orthomodular lattices, which encompass orthocomplemented lattices, and introduce a method to represent any such lattice as a collection of subspaces within a vector space. This method enables the geometric description of all such lattices of a given type, determined by its smallest and largest elements. Moreover, we demonstrate that the mapping between a lattice and its corresponding subspaces is a one-to-one correspondence.

We introduce a visual proof assistant plugin, built on top of Coq, that transforms visual proof strategies introduced in our prior research into a functional visual proof scripts. These scripts can be displayed within the web-based proof viewer, offering an alternative to conventional text-based proof scripts.

We establish a highly accurate upper limit for the maximum fourth moment of normalized analytic Hecke cusp forms when the degree of the polynomial is up to a certain degree and the parameter $T$ does not exceed $10^{15}$. By achieving this bound, we confirm a conjecture proposed by Soundararajan and back it with evidence of the inequality being substantially strict in nature. Our approach involves combining analytic and arithmetic techniques in a novel way in solving the analytic problem.

In the Interior Point Method (IPM), solving linear equations via Iterative Solvers (IS) plays a crucial role for large-scale Linear Programming problems to maintain computational efficiency. However, incorporating IPM with IS leads to variable iteration costs, thereby increasing the overall solution time. This research introduces a novel resolution to this issue by developing a special termination criterion (TCC) for the Krylov solver used in the Primal-Dual Interior-Feasible (PDFF) method. Unlike conventional termination conditions, this approach considers multiple error indicators simultaneously to achieve optimal cost per Simplex method iterations. Extensive testing with different problem sets has demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed model in reducing the total solution time to a substantial extent.

We present the first calculation of a specific component, denoted as $A_{gq}^{(3),L}(N)$, of the leading and second-order twisted states for quarks or gluons, for a given value of $N$. This component is a matrix element of the group of all possible parton distributions and is particularly interesting for odd values of $N$. This finding is an important step in a larger goal, which involves determining all contributions of odd-parity to the second moment of $g_2(x,x_T)$ with a more precise level of understanding.

One critical aspect significantly influencing an AI system's real-world effectiveness is its operational context. Unfortunately, many prominent AI incidents involving real-world deployments are not just unique but also frequently overlooked. A current challenge in the AI research community is the lack of comprehensive AI incident databases. Unlike hardware or software components, there is no standardized method for collecting AI-related incidents. To address this issue, we have developed an incident database specifically tailored for capturing AI failures and mishaps. This repository will facilitate a broader range of research in AI by facilitating comparative analyses of incident frequencies. Furthermore, it can help researchers gain a better understanding of prevalent problems in various AI applications and the real-world limitations of existing AI technologies. This repository is open to contributions, encouraging collaborations with the AI research community to promote greater AI accountability. AI developers, researchers, and evaluators are invited to partner with us in producing related research publications.

We've developed an accurate method for solving renormalization group equations by adapting gradient descent. This approach allows us to clearly visualize the renormalization group flow in complex, high-dimensional systems. Using this method in detail on a standard $\phi^4$ theory in six dimensions, we'll showcase its effectiveness and explain how it revolutionizes our understanding of RG fixed points and their basins of attraction.

Human interaction design often relies on dual-process specifications that ensure safety and liveness requirements are met during human systems operation. Despite their importance, developing efficient techniques to detect and resolve violations of these specifications remains a significant challenge, particularly due to the time constraints of real-time system interactions. This research presents a new methodology based on automata theory for automatically detecting and managing conflicts arising from dual-process specifications in real-time systems. The method enables the designer to customize conflict management strategies by specifying preferences, and ultimately generates a software interface that runs on the system and prompts the user to adhere to the specifications or facilitates dispute resolution through controlled interventions. Demonstrations using two distinct case studies illustrate the practical application and effectiveness of this methodology.

We define the computational model for the Proto-Quantum compiler front-end, Proto-Quipper-M. This language is a high-level programming language designed to create efficient circuits through compositional design, balancing expressiveness and implementability. Our work precisely characterizes the language's structure and computation to aid in understanding its underlying computations. We demonstrate the soundness of our characterization by showing that every program's behavior aligns with our defined model.

The unregularized inverse of a random matrix provides a model for the unregularized empirical Bayes estimator when analyzing large datasets. Its eigenvalues and eigenvectors are also of significant interest due to their unique properties arising from the singular nature of data. We investigate the asymptotic distribution of the bulk, inorganic, and outlying eigenvalues of unregularized inverse matrices formed from data drawn from a large class of stochastic finite-dimensional Gaussian ensembles. Our results are based on the asymptotic eigenvalue distribution of the corresponding stochastic matrix and the corresponding sigmoidal transformation of data. In comparison to the eigenvalue distribution of original data, inorganic and outlier scales in the unregularized inverse are respectively defined by the $-1/\alpha$ and $-2$ scales of data, where $\alpha>0$ represents the exponent of density vanishing at the origin in models with positive support. Data with symmetrically decreasing density exhibit a zero-mean model with a regularized inverse scale, and an infinite eigenspectrum corresponding to density's zero support. Data with heavier tails, however, lead to a regularized eigenvalue transition, in addition to the inorganic and outlier scales. The eigenvector behavior associated with inorganic and outlier spectra also exhibits distinct features, characterized by a Leverage-Scale with localization, and a corresponding Markovian character corresponding to the support of the original data.

A novel method is proposed for producing optical photons through the interaction of two atoms with a cavity, employing a coherent state of light. The atoms, in a coherent state, interact with the cavity, using its high-Q factor for phase measurements. The scheme achieves the creation of entangled photon pairs and squeezed states within the infrared and visible spectra, respectively, from the decay of the atomic excitation. The atoms' coherence is extended over several milliseconds due to the inertial properties of the ground states in which they decay. The idea builds upon the principles of Rydberg blockade, substituting high-lying Rydberg states with dipole states. The proposed system offers advantages, such as the ability to produce photons in the same spatial mode, coherent control of two-boson generation, and the use of long-lived matter coherence.

As assembly genomes grow larger and more complex, computational limitations begin to hinder the process, particularly when multiple cores access memory. Breaking point by point, a novel approach named DPCA overcomes this constraint and enables efficient multi-node calculations.
