The success of pre-training in a wide variety of domains has significantly accelerated advances in natural language processing and related fields. The ability of pretraining to help models perform well on new, unseen tasks through in-context learning has been particularly advantageous. Our study delves into a yet underexplored aspect: the significant influence of pretraining data on a model's capacity for in-context learning with complex tasks such as reasoning. We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of pretraining datasets and their impact on the capability of various language models to engage with datasets such as Game of Life and Rule Set 1, focusing specifically on their ability to learn and apply novel rules. Our analysis utilized a standardized evaluation framework and a novel metric called Z-score standardization to compare the zero-shot and few-shot performance of top models from the model zoo. Our results indicate that a model's pretraining significantly affects its ability to tackle new tasks, and we offer potential explanations for this phenomenon. This research contributes to a systematic understanding of the pretraining process and its impact on the development of few-shot learning capabilities in models.

Computer simulations are used to recreate the behavior of the interstellar medium in different environmental settings, including the influence of cooling, magnetic fields, and the compression of gases. Two types of simulations are performed, one using simulations without sub-grid models, which capture collisions between molecules, and another using simulations with sub-grid models, including the effect of compounds that transfer heat. It's discovered that simulations without sub-grid models result in a lack of stability, while simulations with sub-grid models produce stable clouds analogous to those observed in actual observations from space telescopes. Moreover, simulations with sub-grid models produce stable clouds analogous in size to those found in clusters of galaxies, even when accounting for the effect of compounds that transfer heat. It's also noted that future simulations should take into account fields of magnetic influence to better understand how they affect the stability of clouds in groups of galaxies.

The field of quantum chromodynamics has recently encountered an intriguing and as-yet unexplained phenomenon - the potential for CP violation in the beauty sector.  This discovery, however, has faced resistance as several experiments to date have not provided clear evidence to this effect and as theoretical models predict a relatively low likelihood of this occurrence.  Despite these challenges, the possibility remains that the link between CP violation in beauty and elegance can be established through further investigation using more refined theoretical models and by analyzing how the problem behaves under simplified assumptions.  One such simplification involves replacing a given mathematical expression with one that obeys the rules of an Abelian theory rather than the current non-Abelian version, which in effect makes the two expressions indistinguishable when they contain the same symbols for structure constants.  Ultimately, the connection between CP violation in beauty and elegance may provide a clue as to how to resolve the enigmatic relationship between CP symmetry and its apparent absence in certain physical interactions.

Expanding upon the work of Harris and Schmidt, our research delves into the study of how external strings interact within a specific framework of string theory. We focus on 4-coloring patterns in a specific graphical representation of string theory, known as a world-sheet. Our findings reveal that the initial hypothesis put forth by Gross and the subsequent generalized hypothesis by Harris and Schmidt do not hold up in the context of the specific string theory under examination, which pertains to a particular variant of superstring theory. Interestingly, our research does yield positive results regarding the application of generalized hypotheses in theories involving fermionic strings. Moreover, our study also examines the implications of the hypotheses when applied to the fundamental scattering amplitudes that form the cornerstone of superstring theory.

As the 5G technology nears completion, its vast array of applications and services will soon be in demand from various customers. To accommodate these needs, 5G base stations will be densely deployed across diverse environments, resulting in a rapidly expanding 5G core network that requires careful management. To adapt, 5G core network operators need new tools and strategies to optimize the performance, efficiency, and cost effectiveness of their networks. This study presents an innovative framework for 5G core network management, based on modern control theory and computer science principles, to provide useful and actionable insights for network managers. The proposed framework draws inspiration from self-regulating systems, like the human body's homeostatic balance, to ensure the 5G core network remains functional and adaptable. The presented model has been validated through a simulated attack on 5G core components, demonstrating the proposed management strategies' ability to protect the network from disruptions.

A system that generates realistic voice recordings from scratch using only a single example of each speaker is proposed. Building on the techniques of one-two shot face synthesis, this innovative approach relies on one example from the desired speaker and a vast collection of speakers. The algorithm uses the acoustic manifestations of linguistic information in the single example of the desired speaker to inform a latent representation, from which the desired speech is synthesized. The quality of the output can be further customized by selecting and copying appropriate acoustic units or segments from a large collection of other speakers. Consequently, this method enables the production of high-quality speech recordings for new speakers with minimal input. Compared to existing methods, the proposed algorithm yields more natural and realistic voice recordings.

Optimizing robotic movements in environments with complex obstacles often encounters the challenging issue of non-convexity. Using a data-driven method that applies the McCormick envelope, we tackle this issue by creating multiple sub-problems to find the optimal solution. Experimental results from various test cases, involving a robotic arm avoiding collisions and a robot navigating an environment with moving entities and narrow passages, show that our method finds a good initial solution. However, the method struggles with highly complex problems. Using the obtained solution as a starting point for a standard method improves performance and speed.

Quantum states can be transformed into one another through quantum stochastic channels, which are essentially noise affecting the original state. In this context, mathematical concepts called majorization place strict limitations on which transformations are possible. This paper explores how these mathematical constraints apply to quantum mechanics, confirming that the existing rules are the absolute best possible. By demonstrating the rules' practical use in quantum communication, we show that there are specific cases where smaller outputs cannot be obtained from larger inputs, even with the help of additional quantum data. This paper also shows that the original state's knowledge or measurements can make certain approximations more feasible. Finally, we discuss how majorization rules apply to quantum measurement outcomes, revealing new insights about the underlying mathematical principles.

When we tilt a cup of coffee, the liquid flows from the lower to the higher side along the tilt's plane, creating a curved surface. This shape induces a centrifugal force that counters the tilting effect, causing the coffee to behave like a suspended, slightly irregular pendulum. As a result, the coffee's surface mirrors a pendulum's motion, displaying a noticeable swing-period dependence on its curvature.

Decentralized machine learning is becoming increasingly significant in various fields such as distributed IoT networks and wireless communication systems. By using Decentralized Machine Learning, information can be shared among neighboring nodes in a graph without any node requiring data aggregation, making it robust against communication failures and biases. Despite its advantages, DR-SGD, the dominant decentralized learning algorithm, can be susceptible to topological errors and data distribution shifts. Introducing significant improvements, our work presents a novel method, DR-DSGD, that addresses these vulnerabilities and enhances the reliability of decentralized learning on graphs. Experimental confirmations using real-world datasets demonstrate the reliability and robustness of our method in the face of distribution shifts, graph errors, and attacks such as Eclipse and Sybil scenarios. Furthermore, theoretical analysis provides insights into the convergence of our algorithm under these challenging distributions. By comparing the effects of different network topologies and data distributions, our analysis confirms the reliability and scalability of our approach.

In high-energy nuclear collisions, the number of particles created might be influenced by the energy stored in the initial conditions. We investigated how long-lived magnetic puffs, formed by charged particles interacting with the quark-gluon plasma, affect the condition of energy in the initial stages. The results show that a portion of the energy is converted into magnetic puffs, which can generate a small number of additional particles. However, a significant modification to the particle distribution at high momenta is observed. It's also revealed that the magnetic puffs generate more particles than expected based on thermodynamics. This effect should be visible in the future electron-positron collision experiments at the Large Hadron Collider.

Observations from the ALMA telescope have observed bi-directional flows in nascent stars, such as SOO-RS 2, which possess complex and twisted structures. It's surprising that these low-speed outflows seem to move quicker in certain areas, which contradicts the typical expectation that they should travel faster further from their source. To resolve this anomaly, we've utilized a 3D hydrodynamic simulation to investigate the behavior of these low-speed outflows and their interactions with high-speed material. Our study utilized existing data and applied it to both a unidirectional flow and the actual image data of SOO-RS 2, accounting for its intricate shape. Our analysis demonstrates that when these low-speed outflows interact with the surrounding dense material, they expand and transfer momentum to the material in the actual image match that we've found to be possible if the outflow source moved to a different location. It's therefore possible that the observed features in the outflow are created and modified by interactions with denser material, which may also be possible that the outflow source moves to a different location, to a further distance.

This research develops a theoretical framework that examines the interplay between myelin and axon efficiency in neurons. Initially, we create a model that accounts for spatial equilibrium in axons but simplifies other dimensions. Next, we develop a dynamic model that reflects temporal changes and uses free energy as a core principle. Our analysis demonstrates the existence of two stable states: one characterized by high levels of both molecules and the other by the predominance of one molecule over the other. Through further investigation, we demonstrate that cooperative interactions are essential for mutual proliferation, while a specific mechanism called equibilibrium enables the efficient distribution of molecules. This mechanism is also shown to provide robust outcomes with respect to different input concentrations.

Key resonances affecting the long-term orbits of solar sails occur due to various factors, and two of them, known as Halas-style and Einstein-style resonances, have distinct characteristics. Researchers have developed specific techniques to identify these resonances, and one such technique is being adapted for analyzing the behavior of missions like Decade of a Solar Sail and DE-STAR. Ultimately, analytical methods will provide valuable insights necessary for designing future projects.

A method is presented for creating tight-binding models from first-principles calculations that preserve the measure. The proposed model accounts for both the dynamics of electrons and photons, thus light-matter interactions are included within the framework. The transition from a real-space to a periodic Hamiltonian results in a measure-invariant Tight-Binding model that generates the same statistical properties as its starting point, specifically electronic and photonic correlations. A approach for assessing light-matter interactions has been developed using a light-on/light-off ratio, demonstrating its application in computing the optical properties of a silicon crystal and confirming alignment with existing tight-binding models and experimental data.

My research focuses on robust category-specific object perception that can effectively identify and analyze objects in various environments. While achieving this goal in abstract terms is straightforward, the practical applications face significant challenges due to the complex nature of objects and the noise present in available data. To tackle these issues, I will examine two main scenarios: visual object recognition from 2D images and comprehensive object analysis from 3D point clouds combined with 2D images. Specifically, I will investigate the underlying characteristics of these scenarios, design innovative network architectures, and develop novel training strategies. Notably, to address the problem of missing information and potential noise in 3D data, I will explore an approach that can make the most of two-dimensional images and three-dimensional keypoints. This research will contribute to the advancement of object perception technology and its practical applications in real-world scenarios.

This study introduces a set of iterative procedures to establish the regions of acceptance for squared and linear constraints based on Cauchy-distributed distributions. The region estimation methodology employs a frequency counting approach, leveraging an pre-determined confidence level. The designed algorithm enables the construction of linear and nonlinear confidence intervals for Cauchy distribution parameters.

A type of clinical trial, known as the basket trial, groups similar patients into subsets and tests them against the same treatment(s). These trials utilize two primary statistical designs: one compares response rates and the other focuses on response proportions. A key challenge arises in determining the sample size for each arm, which, when there are multiple arms sharing treatments, creates opportunities to share information between groups. To address this challenge and improve statistical efficiency, we employ Bayesian methods by defining shared hyperparameters across groups and using them to inform sample size calculations. These methods successfully increase effect size estimates and consequently increase the calculated sample sizes when treating multiple unrelated groups of patients. We will demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed Bayesian approaches in comparison to traditional frequentent methods and any information-sharing across groups, through various simulated basket trial scenarios for both response rate and novel response proportion designs.

To meet the growing demand for precision in automation systems, advanced control systems are required. By incorporating parameters into control systems, Performance Improvementmaneuvers (PI) controllers can adapt to various operating conditions. However, the increasing complexity of these systems makes stability verification challenging. A proposed solution is to sequentially shut down the motion control system, checking stability at each step to ensure robustness across all operating conditions. This method was adapted for use with Linear Parameter-Varying (LPV) controllers in high-precision motion systems. We developed a numerical search for LPV trajectories and formulated constraints to ensure the stability of the closed-loop control system. By taking into account uncertainties and parameter variations, robust performance can be achieved despite limited knowledge of the system. This chapter demonstrates the synthesis of an LPV controller with scheduled gains for a piezo-actuated micro-positioner and verifies its effectiveness with an accelerating accelerometer.

Deep learning models, like the ones used for partial-to-partial matching, have revolutionized computer vision by achieving remarkable success in complex tasks. Despite this success, a significant limitation remains due to the requirement for complete object information in traditional methods. As a result, these models struggle when presented with only local subregions. To address this issue, we introduce a self-guided learning framework called Reinforcement-Mediated Attention Network (PRNet), which enables end-to-end alignment of local subregions on 3D shapes. By treating guidance selection and feature extraction as iterative refinement processes, PRNet dynamically enhances the most informative handcrafted descriptors and generates aligned point clouds. Furthermore, our framework's effectiveness can be further amplified through recurrent structure and attention mechanisms that focus on handcrafted descriptors. Extensive experiments validate the superiority of PRNet over state-of-the-art methods on widely-used benchmark datasets.

A group exhibits the $R_\infty$ characteristic if each mapping invariant under genus zero nilpotte BM-Solitar group structures leads to an infinite count of isomorphic components. This paper explores the $R_\infty$ characteristic in relation to certain groups. Initially, it demonstrates that the quotient of the Baumslag-Solitar group $BS(2,3)$ by its lower central series' second term possesses the $R_\infty$ characteristic. Subsequently, it establishes that a specific nilpotte BM-Solitar group structure over a field of characteristic zero possesses the $R_\infty$ characteristic for all possible levels of the quotient.

Most analyses of the Standard Model predict instability in its vacuum, suggesting it may transition to a lower-energy vacuum at around $10^{34}$ cm at a vast and distant time scale of around $10^{100}$ years. This exceptional scenario isn't the only possibility; a less extreme scale for the instability could be around $10^{10}$ to $10^{13}$ years, potentially observable through nucleon decay or particle production in cosmic ray collisions. If the instability scale falls within the range of $10^{13}$ to $10^{16}$ years, future high-energy collider projects like a 3- to $10$-TeV electron-positron collider or a $100$-TeV proton-proton collider could potentially recreate the conditions present at the onset of the big bang.

A novel, robust method has been developed to reverse the effects of momentum smearing in resonant inelastic X-ray scattering spectra, thereby momentum-resolving the resolution. This was achieved by adapting the trajectory framework typically used for electron diffraction and applying it to resonant inelastic X-ray scattering. During momentum smearing, rapid electron motion is blurred due to its finite lifetime. Therefore, the target trajectory framework simulates electron propagation, accounting for its lifetime until the observed scattering pattern is matched. We successfully applied this method to model the argon and doped skantra trajectory framework, and the results show that it resolves the momentum smearing and provides clear observation of the transfer of valence and core holes along with the trajectory framework

We employ the Bethe-Salpeter equation to obtain the momentum distribution of charged particles in the charmed mesons D and DS. By solving this equation non-perturbatively using the lattice formulation, we derive the density functions of these mesons and uses them as tool for distinguishing between different excited states D2 and DS2 through density characteristics and validate our results with existing experimental data on form factors D and L using light-by-light scattering processes.

We derive precise Fourier transformations that map between Gelfand-Shilov spaces, circumventing traditional methods by employing an indirect four-step procedure. This allows us to bypass high-computation techniques such as repeated differentiation, smoothing, and non-classical bracket operations. Instead, our approach relies on the structural properties of these spaces and their compatibility with the Fourier transform. Additionally, this precise Fourier transform proves useful in analyzing the Toeplitz operator on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, revealing properties of semi-classical Toeplitz matrices that reflect the non-ordinary nature of Gelfand-Shilov spaces.

In the realm of semi-supervised learning, the advent of multimodal data has presented both opportunities and difficulties. Although existing methods for image and text-based supervision have shown some success, they frequently falter when confronted with diverse instance types of concurrent modalities. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a novel approach, Cyclic Division GAN, for partitioning distinct multimodal instance categories in an unsupervised manner. Cyclic Division GAN employs the cyclic consistency principle to develop a gan that captures shared latent representations for disparate modalities, using only unlabeled data. By capturing modal-specific nuances through encoder-decoder architectures and leveraging a combination of cycle loss and classification loss, we enhance the representation quality required for instance-level partitioning. The resulting instance-level discriminator evaluates the authenticity of modality labels, serving as a critical component for multilevel partitioning across modality spaces. We support our proposed method with experimental results on three comprehensive benchmark datasets, demonstrating its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art alternatives.

To precisely anticipate a agent's movement in a virtual environment, we must first decode the probability distributions of its actions, which can be extracted from observed sensory inputs. A novel end-to-end model has been developed to achieve action prediction by combining two key components: 1) utilizing an improved, radial basis function-based neural network to extract actionable features from complex input data, and 2) incorporating long short-term memory cells within the feature-based prediction model. Our proposed model has shown significant improvement in predicting human walking directions when only limited visual information is available. Additionally, the radial basis function-based feature extraction approach has demonstrated adaptable performance across various action prediction tasks.

A simulation of NIR and MIR data from AD Leo's 1985 UV to X-ray eruption was conducted, utilizing the HERMES code for ERADiation emission. The setup is similar to Watson et al's (2019) work, with an expanded analysis of the accretion column and a broader wavelength range. The study assumes a magnetized T Tauri star with its accretion rate and stellar field strength adjusted to match observed NIR and MIR data, then compares computed and measured spectra. After an initial phase of an accretion shock dominance, the accretion column becomes obscured by an expanding dust cloud clump. The accretion column re-emerges following the dispersal or migration of the dust, resulting in enhanced ad hoc stellar and disc continuum emission measurements relative to pre-eruptive levels. In a contrasting scenario, a significantly stronger stellar magnetosphere is identified through elevated NIR and MIR rates and decreased NIR variability. The accretion column dominates in a broad wavelength range from UV to IR. The analysis concludes with an examination of how this model differs when applied to other, notably higher-stellar-mass objects.

We are investigating the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2 manifolds. A general framework for analyzing deformations of geometric objects is presented, which enables us to define the deformation complex for nearly G2 instantons. This framework reveals that the space of first-order deformations of nearly G2 instantons is not necessarily associative, but it does possess the properties of symmetry and associativity. As a specific application of our framework, we demonstrate that the deformation complex for nearly G2 instantons coincides with the Chern-Simons complex when the nearly G2 structure arises from a spinors.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a particular condition under the action of a conjugation operation. This condition can be rephrased as $T$ satisfying a similar condition with respect to a Hermitian operation. We will investigate the conditions under which C-normal weighted composition operators on the Hardy space of analytic functions map between two given analytic functions.

We've developed an approach to count all 2-core $2^n$-compositions of an even number for any $n \ge 1$. Utilizing this method, we've derived a recursive formula with a closed-form closed fencing device. Furthermore, generalizing this method, we've created a framework for counting all $p^n$-core $p'^n$-compositions of an even number for any prime $p$ and exponent $e \ge 1$. We've explained the relationship between these core compositions and a type of stroll on the additive residue graph of a prime $p$ or power of a prime $p$.

The goal of point cloud segmentation is to classify each point in a 3D scene to belong to a specific category. Effective segmentation often relies on using various 3D representations of clouds, such as points, voxels, and surfaces, but combining them solely based on fixed strategies yields suboptimal results when some forms are noisy or inaccurate. Our proposed solution involves integrating the strengths of multiple smoothening approaches through a flexible framework called TPC that applies various transformations to cloud representations before fusing them based on the specific configuration. Despite showing superior performance on numerous benchmark datasets, the capacity of TPC to handle novel configurations may lead to overfitting, and therefore we refine our approach by evaluating its robustness on several benchmarks and introducing VTPC, a simplified variation. Our techniques establish new state-of-the-art benchmarks on diverse datasets and provide clear insights for further research in 3D point segmentation. The code and models for TPC and VTPC are freely accessible at https://github.com/robinfrees/tpc.

We investigate the application of medium access control protocols in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks to mitigate interference between radar units and explore the feasibility of utilizing these protocols to gather and process network information. A novel medium access control scheme designed for FMCW networks builds upon Slotted ALOHA principles. This scheme introduces two innovative features: (a) the capability to determine and limit the network size, thereby allowing the network coordinator to calculate access probabilities for each node; (b) the ability to collect and monitor the number of active nodes. Furthermore, the probability of active nodes can be optimized for maximum stability through an optimized search method. A second proposed protocol is an adaptation of Distance-Related (DRT) Time Division Multiple Access (TDMA), which generates dynamic spatial maps of the network. A comparative analysis of these three medium access control schemes is presented.

Our research investigates entangled photon pairs generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion and assessed at both quantum and quantum-like levels, specifically focusing on their behavior in the famous Hong-Ou-Mandel experiment. We trace the development of these photon states from their initial creation to the final spectral analysis. Furthermore, we examine the behavior of entangled photons as they interact with a non-linear substance, known as entangled photon absorption, and assess how this interaction impacts the Hong-Ou-Mandel interference pattern. We also explore the behavior of these photons when measured after quantum interactions using quantum tomography.

We establish an isomorphism between the elliptic cohomology of complex matrices in the local limit and that of complex vectors in the elliptic cohomology theory with complex K-theory moduli space, specifically for T^2/L math. This work involves developing a T^k/L math -equivariant elliptic cohomology for complex matrices and proving its isotopy invariant and structure for the local limit functor. Moreover, we derive the elliptic cohomology theory for complex matrices based on the generalized Atiyah-Singer index theorem for T^k/L math -equivariant maps and express its representation as the sum of the indices of holomorphic sections.

Temporal knowledge graph representation learning has limitations due to the large number of parameters in neural network models, which also leads to a lack of connection between different models. This research focuses on developing a low-rank representation for temporal knowledge graphs that reduces model dependencies. By employing a two-step approach, first a preliminary representation is learned from data with limited information and then a refinement stage incorporates prior model knowledge, a compatible high-order tensor decomposition method is used for both sparse data and integrated models. Through comprehensive evaluations on various datasets, it has been demonstrated that this low-rank representation outperforms other methods in terms of knowledge graph embedding and temporal inference.

In the context of noisy ground states affecting computational performance, several key questions emerge. Firstly, does ground noise influence the computational process? Secondly, does it serve as a barrier to computation across various computational models? Thirdly, does it constitute an inherent limitation or just a temporary problem with implementational details? Our analysis reveals that primed systems, which are systems initialized in an excited state, provide insight into this problem. As they evolve over time, primed systems can be viewed as an exponentially shrinking error rate, offering a robust solution. This concept is further applied to demonstrate the feasibility of implementing Turing machines without error, despite the presence of ground noise. Additionally, similar ideas are used to design Turing machines that automatically recognize regular languages in real-time without errors.

A celebrated phenomenon, the violation of local realism without inequalities, is demonstrated through the relationship between its degree of perfection and a specific non-linear, non-bijective function applied to the correlation data from experiment. This relationship holds true even with imperfect data. When experiments yield imperfect correlations, a precise mathematical operation, the Chebyshev distance between related matrices, can accurately reflect the extent of these correlations. This distance is directly proportional to the degree of a highly nonlinear transformation applied to the correlations, thus quantifying their value.

In the realm of quantum transport, flat bands and isolated energy states often contribute significantly to understanding the property's behavior. Traditionally, flat bands are associated with localized wave functions, which then dominate others due to their unique characteristics, according to the notion introduced by Okamoto and Kozina. Our research endeavors to dissect this connection between flat bands and localization, which historically received little exploration. To achieve this goal, we developed a flat-band indicator that measures the wave functions' conformity with the infinite potential barrier approximation, effectively quantifying their degree of localization. Utilizing mathematical proofs and numerical examples of multiband systems, we demonstrate that wave functions derived under this approximation, while measuring conformality effectively, fail to fully capture actual confinement. Consequently, we argue that conformality and confinement are distinct concepts that cannot be equated. Furthermore, we expose the underlying limitation of the conformity metric as the primary reason for this shortcoming. Additionally, we introduce a corrective formula to better approximate the actual confinement time of wave packets.

Recent studies of $T_c$ records in superconductors have led to the belief that third-generation superconductors -- comprised of dense electron-carrier metal hydrides -- will possess an even higher $T_c$.  The highly conductive metal hydride TnH₂ ($n = 2$ or 3) was claimed to be responsible for a $100\,\mathrm{K}$ $T_c$ under $27\,\mathrm{TPa}$ pressure in 2019.  However, the discovery's credibility has given rise to significant controversy.  Researchers have extensively analyzed the $h$-atom's role in hydrides' electronic structure using various models.  This study offers an alternative perspective, demonstrating the $h$-atom's insignificant impact on the electronic properties of $n = 2$ or 3 metal hydrides due to strong covalent bonding with surrounding $h$-atoms.  As a result, the $h$-atom's removal yields an essentially insulating molecular system, indicating that hydrides' high $T_c$ is unlikely due to Bazarov's theory.  This finding also applies to other potential high-$T_c$ recorders, such as MgB₂ and Sn, and suggests that any new recorders will have a more similar insulating character.  Despite these limitations, Bazarov's model may still accurately describe the effect of $h$-atoms on the $T_c
Execute an element-wise operation on the array \texttt{a}, returning the result starting from index \texttt{start} up to \texttt{end}, applying the function \texttt{op} to each element.

We derive precise requirements for a group to be the fundamental group of a projective or affine variety, utilizing this criterion to charcterize arithmetic groups, demonstrating that they are precisely the finite index subgroups within these groups. The concept of a projective group is one subsumed by the idea of a charmability, which in turn, is part of a broader class of rigid groups, defined as having a finite number of cohomology in low degrees for any finite coefficient module. The proof relies on a novel application of purity in cohomology with constant local tori, enabling us to adapt a topology-theoretic approach originally used by S. Lichtenbaum for number rings, providing an alternative to the original proof, which in turn, relied on the theory of automorphic forms by building on the pioneering work of Godement and Hecke.

Self-driving cars use complex systems with numerous sensors to operate safely. 
Lidar technology provides precise distance data, which is utilized in various 
applications like mapping the surroundings and detecting obstacles. However, 
the integration of Lidar into these systems raises concerns about validation 
and reliability. This study presents the verification of a high-level 
fail-operational system designed for detecting and responding to obstacles 
using a fail-safe approach. The fail-safe mechanism is activated when specific 
conditions are met, for example when multiple consecutive Lidar readings show 
no obstacles within a specified distance. A TextX configuration parser 
parses a user-defined configuration and text, which includes a fail-safe 
system setup and critical parameters, to create a fail-safe detector model. The 
model undergoes formal verification using model checking with NuSMV, which 
demonstrates the reliability of the fail-safe detector.

The stability of nonlinear systems can be assessed through the use of impact-based clustering of their phase space, which highlights areas of interest such as attractors and repellers. Despite various algorithms being proposed for this purpose, a comprehensive review of their performance on a comprehensive set of openly accessible datasets is still lacking. In this study, we present an data-driven approach to partition a given set of phase space using a specific algorithm, known as the nearest neighbor algorithm, and demonstrate that it effectively identifies areas of interest such as attractors and repellers. Following this development, we conduct an in-depth evaluation of impact-based clustering algorithms by partitioning a large collection of datasets and analyzing their efficacy. A key outcome of this study is the generation of a detailed benchmark table that outlines the performance of each clustering method on every dataset and its associated confidence level. This benchmark serves as a useful guide for selecting an appropriate algorithm when investigating a newly encountered nonlinear system.

This paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the diverse approaches to Leibnizian infinitesimal analysis by comparing the strengths and weaknesses of three prevalent methodologies - infinitesimal monads, $\epsilon$-infinite nets, and Keisler fields. The paper begins by defining what constitutes infinitesimal analysis in the Leibnizian sense. It then examines the first approach, exploring its historical background and mathematical foundations, before assessing its current merits. A similar examination is conducted for the second approach, known as nonstandard analysis, highlighting its relationship to the first approach and a distinct variant. Finally, the paper discusses a third approach, involving alternative mathematical structures, by contrasting it with the first two approaches.

Using the disturbance theory, we've calculated the HI intensity mapping power spectrum for a specific large-scale structure, focusing on how it changes based on the background subtraction method employed. The theoretical predictions are then compared with a set of high-resolution N-body simulations that include HI signals, and the applicable redshift range is identified. Additionally, the constraints on the bias parameters are established by incorporating a logarithmic bias model for low redshift scenarios and a redshift-dependent bias model for higher redshifts within the constraints of our simulations. Finally, the impact of background subtraction on the bias parameters and data points is assessed, and two commonly used subtraction methods are found to significantly reduce bias and eliminate certain data points for certain redshifts, which may need to be further considered in the analysis of real data.

A newStueckelberg mechanism functions as a gravity St\"uckelberg mechanism that successively decouples the gravitational equations in each spacetime step. The theory remains fully consistent in an infinite dimensional spacetime where it can be described using operators that commute.

Recommender systems, a key component behind our daily online experiences, analyze user-preferred items to suggest new ones. However, two major issues persist in this field: enhancing the quality of recommendations and reducing the cold-start problem where new users/items receive few interactions. Researchers have applied deep learning to improve recommendations but often neglect the benefits of traditional collaborative filtering, leading to unsatisfying outcomes when combining the two. In this paper, we explore a unified approach by examining two distinct types of techniques - context-based and behavior-based methods. Our framework identifies their limitations and proposes behavior-based methods as suitable for handling user-preferred item data. We experimented with both approaches on a real-world e-commerce dataset and found context-based techniques to excel at profiling user preferences from sparse data, whereas behavior-based methods demonstrate superior performance when ample interaction data is available for the target item.

We investigate a matrix group in noncommutative probability and identify a novel property for a matrix type, showing equivalence between two interpretations of this property - one from a kind B freeness perspective, and another from a 2x2 conditional independence perspective when matrices are freely independent of a specific kind.

In order to effectively verify the accuracy of real-time systems, especially when it comes to monitoring their safety liveness properties as well as temporal characteristics like periodicity, it's essential to have a comprehensive approach. This study puts forth a logical framework, modeled after the LTL (Linear Temporal Logic) framework, but tailored for capturing the unique characteristics of timed systems by introducing four key operators. These operators enhance existing logical frameworks with operators for checking if an event occurs exactly once, repeatedly, within a certain time frame, and also within a specific time frame. Furthermore, this research demonstrates how to define a model-based semantics for such an enriched framework, as well as a characterisation of its associated syntax through a characterisation of its associated syntax. Additionally, it is shown that the enriched framework is capable of describing timed characteristics, thus providing a useful tool for checking timed requirements. Moreover, the research highlights the usefulness of this framework by providing algorithms for determining whether a given formula is satisfiable. Lastly, the research examines the computational complexity of the associated model-based semantics, demonstrating that it is at most complexity.

The decay process $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi \pi^0 \eta$ is examined, and it is determined that this process can occur through two avenues: the $a_0(980)-f_0(980)$ intertwining effect or as a direct production. Utilizing the analytic continuation of the Green function in quantum field theory enables the identification and separation of two-dimensional interference patterns associated with the resonances $a_0(980)$ and $f_0(980)$ in the $\pi^0 \eta$ channel. Our research reveals that the quark-antiquark annihilation route is the primary driver for the transition of a $c\bar c$-like resonance to scalar mesons, with unique features of this process serving as a valuable tool for understanding the $a_0(980)-f_0(980)$ mechanism, with a view towards its application at the LHCb experiment.

The GRAVITY capture camera is one of four components making up the GRAVITY instrument for the VLT/ interferometer. Between 2015 and 2017, the camera was primarily utilized in an astrometry study focusing on S2 orbiting the supermassive black hole located at the center of the Milky Way, along with a complementary astrometry assessment of the core's population of old, red stars. Additionally, the camera played a significant role in both studies by accurately determining the relative positions of stars in real-time. As part of GRAVITY's development phase, further applications of the capture camera have also been explored.

We're investigating the effectiveness of approximation algorithms for a broadened version of the k-Center problem, particularly in the context of a metric's doubling dimension and double covering number. Our research demonstrates that approximating the k-Center problem to any degree better than O(log^2 k) represents a computationally challenging task, even when utilizing only black-box access to these properties. Conversely, our findings highlight the difficulty that the metric's intrinsic doubling dimension or double covering number can impose on the k-Center problem, even in the case where such a metric is explicitly provided, with the ability to achieve an approximation ratio no better than Ω(log^2 k). Nonetheless, we offer an approximation algorithm with a guaranteed performance ratio, dependent on these metric's doubling dimension, double covering number, and the radius ratio between the metric's center and its lowest 2k-point center. Furthermore, we offer a simplified, although potentially suboptimal, approximation algorithm with the best-known performance ratio, at  O(log^2 k), even for the standard k-Center problem, even when utilizing only black-box access to these properties, even when a more advanced, quantum access is utilized.

This paper investigates the singularity of $P(z+α)$ within polynomial $P(z)$ and non-zero constant $α$, showing that if $P(z)$ is singular then it must be a finite normal product of distinct irreducible factors that satisfy specific growth and translation discount conditions. Based on this outcome, the paper presents the corresponding result for entire functions and explores singularity connections with respect to $q$-polynomials and $q$-difference functions.

This paper investigates the effects of numerical inaccuracies on polynomial linear system resolution, using a probabilistic model that simulates computation errors like rounding or overflow. The study shows that inaccurate solutions can have major downstream consequences and that certain errors cannot be corrected once they occur. The paper also introduces two key concepts: a novel bound that quantifies when incorrectness becomes unavoidable, and a premature stopping mechanism for iterative resolution methods that prevents compounding mistakes. The proposed mechanisms improve upon earlier methods by offering better assurance of exiting before an irrecoverable mistake happens. The ideas developed here can be applied to various resolution methods such as the Simplex algorithm and Gaussian elimination.

A novel type of photon emission, generated by a driven two-dimensional array of oscillators, has been experimentally verified. This novel photon emission type is protected by parity symmetry and arises from the system's non-Hermitian symmetry, which allows for secure access to a quantum state that is immune to perturbations. This novel photon emission type is a two-dimensional extension of previously reported three-dimensional parity-time symmetry-breaking modes. When the system's parameters traverse a phase transition, the bundle emission, a highly collimated beam of photons, is generated. The probability of finding the system in this state is found to be increased when arranged in two-dimensional and three-dimensional configurations. Additionally, this novel photon emission type has been observed experimentally in a system of cavity coupled superconducting qubits.

We develop a simple yet accurate theoretical model that can be used to describe the thermodynamic behavior of an equilibrium gas composed of atomic species of group I. This model considers processes such as the ionization of neutral atoms and subsequent recombination. It predicts key properties of the atomic group I materials, including their density changes with temperature and pressure, as well as their pressure variations with temperature and density. Furthermore, our model predicts the variation of specific heat with temperature and density for solid, liquid, and gaseous phases. These predictions are generally in line with available experimental and computer simulation studies for lithium, as well an analysis performed for potassium. Notably, our results indicate that specific heat can reach values significantly higher than the specific heat constant Boltzmann's.

The behavior of vector mesons in a chiral-imbalanced environment, created by particle vacuum disparities, is examined at zero temperature using a novel ground-state method for quantum chromodynamics and its extensions that include three- and four-quark interactions. By analyzing the mesonic spectral functions at zero momentum, distinct signals for possible bound states at the level of degrees of freedom are identified. Notably, signal peaks for the $J^PC = 1^{--}$ state, consistent with the $ω$ meson, show significant enhancement in the region of zero frequency due to interactions within the chiral-imbalanced environment.

This research focuses on determining the scale of a network from its connection probabilities, assuming a small-world model with uniform noise and no structure corruption. A proposed method calculates a reliable estimate of network scale, even in the absence of any corruption, by utilizing only the given data and without needing to know the level of noise. A theoretical framework is also established to set an upper limit on estimation errors, which shows that even with noise, the method remains effective to within one standard deviation. Experiments with both artificially created and real-world data confirm that even when up to 10% of the data is corrupted, estimates remain relatively accurate, although their reliability may not be fully accounted for. Interestingly, even with corruption, the method tends to underestimate the true scale, reinforcing its utility in interpreting network data, especially when the method indicates results beyond the graph's maximum possible distance.

A set of novel simulation tools, CTTK, has been created to expand the limited data available in numerical relativity research by creating realistic gravitational wave signals from the merger of black holes. The generated signals accurately represent the complex dynamics of general relativity, and can be used to supplement existing waveforms to improve the performance of gravitational wave detection methods. The strategy of using synthetic data to overcome data scarcity in science has the potential to be applied to other fields as well.

The WangXing experiment, a water-Cherenkov detector located at the MAXLAB in Finland, aims to study neutrino oscillations using radioactive sources. Each of the 32 detectors within the array contains 20 water-equivalent glass panels, monitored by nitrogen-doped xenon photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) attached to the front and back surfaces. To accurately measure and control background noise, a thorough examination of these PMTs is necessary. We conducted a detailed analysis of 20-inch PMTs in terms of their Cherenkov light yield, noise levels, and detection efficiency, specifically for the JUNO experiment's requirements.

Forecasting complex system behavior across various fields like economics, physics, and engineering is an active area of research. The utilization of machine learning models, particularly those based on deep learning, has yielded significant results in this domain. Notably, the Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) has been used to model relationships between time series data, providing a range of solutions for predictions. The multivariate GCN has demonstrated exceptional performance in direct modeling due to its ability to track variable interactions over extended periods. However, the fixed structure of its graph connections may not adequately represent dynamic relationships between variables. This study proposes an enhanced multivariate GCN that dynamically adjusts its structure based on the predicted time steps. The new model introduces an adaptive graph layer that identifies the most relevant variable relationships at each step, thus outperforming existing models in terms of accuracy and interpretability. The proposed model's ability to visually represent its findings also facilitates the identification of the underlying patterns governing temporal variations.

To verify the accuracy of atmospheric radiative transfer models, observations of the sky at night are employed as a natural laboratory. By measuring the brightness of the sky away from stars, instrumental effects and atmospheric effects can be distinguished. A novel technique was developed to isolate instrumental effects from true sky brightness using measurements taken near and far from stars at various wavelengths. High-precision on-the-sky observations were then conducted with the VLT-UVES spectrograph at multiple passbands in the visible and infrared spectrum, during clear nights without moonlight. By comparing measured spectra with theoretical models, parameters such as atmospheric extinction and intrinsic sky brightness were calibrated. Models from various sources were also compared and the CIMOMO model accurately predicted atmospheric scattering at our observatory location. Our research significantly reduces the uncertainty associated with atmospheric correction when observing faint objects, essentially matching the level of uncertainty associated with photon statistics.

Recent advancements in Label Distillation have shown exceptional performance across various challenging scenarios. Currently, most distillation frameworks are designed to be either flexible in adapting to diverse scenarios or effective during complex situations, but rarely both. In this research, we introduce PILE, a PErvasive Logits Ensemble method that overcomes this limitation by providing a unified solution. PILE supports a wide range of scenarios, including complex situations with multiple complex labels. By combining an ML-based complexity metric and a complexity-aware encoder design, PILE effectively handles multiple logits outputs efficiently. Our approach also introduces an innovative iterative log coalition strategy to enhance performance, demonstrating significant enhancements of 2.06 and 1.46 mIoU when compared to current state-of-the-art methods on Cityscapes and Cityvectors datasets.

We introduce a new technique for detecting very light dark matter made of bosons, utilizing a method of gravitational wave measurement through the observation of strength changes. Implementing this technique would involve a sensor comprised of oscillating masses that respond to the oscillating gravitational field generated by the Earth. This approach is capable of sensing ultralight dark matter fields directly, in contrast to other methods that detect their implications on phenomena like the cosmic microwave background radiation, stellar development, or the movement of particles. The proposed system functions as a coherent detector, making it highly sensitive to extremely subtle changes in the gravitational field generated by the Earth. This technique is also compatible with the use of light to monitor the system's performance.

This paper explores the concept of uniqueness for a broad class of problems involving compressed sensing, specifically those formulated through a continuous relationship between observed data and an unknown function. These problems are solved via minimization of either the L1 norm or total variation. Utilizing an infinite-dimensional framework based on measure theory, we demonstrate that the characteristic functions associated with minimal solutions are identifiable when data noise is present within certain bounds and a specific experimental setup is in place. Our findings extend the definition of identifiability for sparse signals from a property related to data and noise being disjoint to one that accounts for network construction and the interaction between noise and signal. This revised interpretation aligns with the long-standing belief in signal analysis that signals with L1 priors are inherently identifiable.

This paper introduces an open-source compiler framework for the P416 network programming language, featuring both the latest P416 language syntax and an advanced backend architecture. Our/compiler framework is designed to take advantage of modern compiler technology, including path exploration and source-level constant evaluation, in order to efficiently generate high-quality VHDL and Verilog output. By leveraging this framework, developers can easily and cost-effectively implement, test, and deploy custom packet processing programs on adjustable match-action table switch architectures.

In the study "Discretising the vector conveyance equation with a quadrilateral
mesh for a superconvergent solution using the Raviart-Thomas element', a novel mesh generation technique based on a regular grid is presented. The research employs the
Raviart-Thomas finite element method coupled with the continuous Galerkin finite element method on this specially designed grid to discretise the vector conveyance equation.
The elements of the resulting system of nonlinear algebraic equations are solved using a Broyden method that achieves rapid convergence. The study demonstrates that this combination of methods yields highly accurate numerical solutions that are in line with theoretical expectations, specifically, the solutions are superconvergent and have fifth-order
local and third global rates of convergence. The accuracy of the computed solutions is also found to be in accordance with the predicted energies errors and is influenced by grid irregularities, with these effects diminishing at lower rates as the solution becomes more precise.

A cutting-edge machine learning technique known as federated learning allows multiple organizations to collaborate on training without sharing sensitive data, maintaining its confidentiality, while preventing any entity from accessing the stored information. However, a SFL model trained using federated learning may inadvertently leak information about the participant's data through its gradient updates, potentially also exposing training characteristics, such as the algorithm and training duration, used during these updates, which could also convey confidential information to participating models. In order to mitigate digital privacy risks associated with gradients and algorithms in SFL, we introduce the notion of differential confidentiality for both the gradient update and the model used in training and develop practical methods for securely implementing federated learning that respects this new definition, ensuring the confidentiality of participating data remains intact.

A cross-section measurement was undertaken for the production of $B_c^+$ mesons at the LHCb experiment, utilizing the 2011-2012 dataset. Analysis in the rest frame of $J/\psi$ led to the discovery of a resonant structure centered at $6.876$ $GeV$, which cannot be attributed to production $B_c$ mesons alone. This notable feature is supported by multiple testing methods and corresponds to a significance of $5\sigma$. As it aligns with theoretical predictions, the observed structure is concluded to be the $3^1S_0$ excited state of $B_c^+$.

This paper presents an innovative Runge-Kutta estimation method for addressing certain differential problems, including initial-value problems and boundary-value problems. The proposed Runge-Kutta method is an advanced continuous estimation technique, built upon a specific class of Runge-Kutta methods known as embedded Runge-Kutta estimators. The technique offers significant advantages, including the concurrent determination of the optimal step-size and global solution estimation. Specifically, it can efficiently solve boundary-value problems using the continuous estimation and an adaptive step-size refinement based on the mesh. The proposed method is demonstrated to be effective with minimal computational overhead, providing global solution estimation without additional calculations, thereby making it a viable option for implementing other numerical solution techniques, such as the shooting method.

A key factor in modern AI breakthroughs is the development of complex neural networks with millions to tens of millions of parameters. By utilizing backpropagation in an end-to-end framework, the performance of neural components can be continuously optimized for various applications such as speech and vision tasks. Nevertheless, extremely large neural networks pose significant challenges for end-to-end end-point learning due to the scarcity of computational resources and sample data for end-to-end endpoint learning. To resolve this issue, we introduce a novel method to resolve this challenge by decoupling the training process and regional learning, and then regionally expanding the learned parameters. We also outline a process for end-to-end evaluation of regions and training regional evaluators to adapt regional neural components to cooperate and work together. This method allows for end-to-end endpoint backpropagation and performance optimization. It is discovered that regional evaluators and regional trainers can accelerate end-to-end endpoint training and performance improvement, and thus region-based training can be used as a valid alternative for end-to-end endpoint training and performance enhancement. It is also noted that this method can be easily extended and applied to multi-machine training scenarios.

Our investigation involves three-dimensional chaotic advection with a wada set in a mixing chamber.  Wada points exist at the boundary between the different trapped vortex regions and the dynamic area where particles are transported by the flow.  Even in a low-viscosity environment where NVE applies, as long as there is some level of viscosity present, the unique wada regions expand at an exponential rate.  The rate at which they expand is slightly above the initial rate seen in a non-viscous setting and is marginally less than the rate seen in a high-viscosity environment where NVE does not apply.  The only factor influencing this three-dimensional phenomenon is the size and shape of the different trapped vortex regions.  These regions are time-invariant in size and shape.  As a result, there is no topological constraint limiting the size of this wada set in three-dimensional systems, which greatly differs from two-dimensional systems where it would be restricted by different trapped regions.  Furthermore, even in a low-viscosity environment where NVE applies, the only factor limiting the size and shape of this wada set is its initial size and shape.

Non-Abelian "axigluons" serve as compelling examples of new particles that could be found at the TeV scale and interact with standard model particles. However, previous research indicated that the lack of observation in flavor-changing neutral meson decays severely limited the possibilities for these particles in direct collisions. Our study reveals that the limitations imposed by neutral meson decay analyses can be largely disregarded for certain non-Abelian light bosons - specifically those that transform as a triplet under SU(3) color. We demonstrate that the neutral decay rates of B and D mesons are unaffected by these specific particles due to the cancellation of their effects. Consequently, the durability of these specific bosons at the LHC becomes considerable, making their detection highly feasible.

This research introduces the Hierarchical Focus Network (HIFU), an innovative approach to visual task resolution, specifically designed for recognizing activities within video segments. Unlike existing methods that assume uniform importance throughout feature sequences, HIFU dynamically prioritizes distinct aspects at different temporal stages. By breaking down the recognition process into two key components - a feature attention model that extracts relevant information from clips, and a temporal attention model that focuses on pivotal frames within the feature sequence - HIFU enhances the recognition of visual tasks. The proposed model's effectiveness is notably demonstrated through superior performance on the NTU-RGB+D 60 and S2U datasets, with a relatively modest computational overhead compared to baseline methods.

In RNAd black holes interacting with a scalar field, we investigate the thermodynamics and confirm the feeble version of cosmic censorship. By adjusting the scalar field parameter and applying the first law of thermodynamics, we calculate the changes in horizon areas and verify that the future event horizon always moves towards or stays at the initial state, thereby confirming the feeble version of cosmic censorship. Furthermore, through our analysis, we find that the specific heat and equation of state vary significantly with the radial distance from the singularity to the outer horizon, demonstrating that the system's thermodynamics is non-constant.

The formation of stars occurs within dense molecular clouds, which are largely invisible in visible light but can be seen in various wavelengths such as X-ray, ultraviolet, and infrared. These observations provide crucial insights into the environment surrounding newly formed stars, particularly those that are hidden from view. Recent space-based missions have successfuly detected this obscured starlight, which has significantly advanced our understanding of star formation processes.

Using the Nested Sampling method, we have derived expressions for both Shannon and Tsallis entropies of a probability distribution within the N-dimensional parameter space. Our results also provide a way to compare the effectiveness of different prior choices.

We provide a framework to analyze measure-valued solutions for first-order nonlinear hyperbolic conservation laws with the aid of a Hamiltonian phase space formulation. Utilizing a combination of the method of characteristics and weak continuity in probability, we prove the existence of such solutions and examine their properties. It's important to note that these solutions capture a broader range of complex dynamical phenomena like vacuum formation and shock consolidation.

The proliferation of IoT devices has accelerated innovation and advancement, yet has also attracted the attention of malicious actors, who can exploit these devices due to their vulnerability. This challenge is compounded by the limited computational resources of embedded systems, which hinders the efficacy of existing intrusion detection systems. A solution to this problem is NBcoded, a resource-efficient, light-weight classifier designed to detect network attacks on IoT devices. NBcoded leverages a pre-trained deep learning model to analyze and reduce packet data, which is then fed into NBcoded's encoder and Naive Bayes model for efficient and accurate attack detection. In comparative tests, NBcoded outperformed other similar solutions, achieving a remarkable 99.95% and 100% detection rate for SYN and UDP floods respectively, while requiring minimal memory resources and time for computation.

This research investigates a linearization issue that arises from a fundamental expansion problem concerning group actions. Building upon a 2002 problem proposed by Joni, a deeper understanding of how a group's action can be extended in a natural way is explored in the context of a solvable group acting on a vector space. The findings reveal that, for a solvable group, the natural expansion of a $G$-module $V$ in a $G\ltimes \mathbb{K}\omega$-module $V\oplus\omega$ correctly increases the rank by one. This holds true whenever $\omega$ is a non-trivial weight of the original module $V$. The validation of a conjecture proposed by Anderson and Joni in the specific case when $G$ is a nilpotent group leads to a comprehensive solution for the general case when $G$ is a solvable group.

To identify movement in video, a computational method has been developed that leverages machine learning techniques, specifically designed to recognize and track biological motion. The model was trained on an extensive dataset of 50 frames arranged in a 2D grid, where each frame contains a moving object and a static background. By analyzing the differences between consecutive frames, the model can pinpoint moving objects in real-time video footage. The underlying theory suggests that organisms have evolved universal patterns of motion that can be captured and recognized through these patterns. The model's performance was tested by analyzing everyday video footage and producing heat maps that highlight the presence of motion. The method's effectiveness in detecting movement was further demonstrated by successfully tracking a falling apple and distinguishing between the motion of different objects. The model's code is available on GitHub for further exploration and reproduction of the findings.

The growing need to optimize energy consumption to combat climate change has led to an increased challenge of finding improved, low-carbon energy alternatives. This work presents a method using QUBO modeling and quantum computing to design better energy distribution networks by substituting local power generation with renewable energy sources, such as solar power, for existing bulk electricity. A QUBO model was developed and tested on a 13-node system and on the larger IEEE 118-bus network, demonstrating successful, cost-effective replacement of conventional power generation with sustainable energy options. Ultimately, this research contributes to efforts addressing the pressing climate crisis by designating climate change as a primary driver for developing an improved energy infrastructure.

Different methods attempt to identify the optimal physical representations of data by being invariant under optimal transformations. We establish a unified framework that explains why these methods find consistent solutions. We apply this method to explain existing physical representations that were previously found using ad hoc methods and also discover new ones. We use the new framework to identify ad invariance methods that are suboptimal and inconsistent. We use variational methods to identify a unified principle driving the formation of stable, reversible, and conserved quantities. We find that spurious physical representations often fail to capture the true dynamics of data and produce unrealistic transformations. We apply our framework to a wide range of tasks, including molecular action recognition, solid-state molecule analysis, and key element extraction from micrographs.

A search for massive particles lasting long after the LHC's collisions was done at 13 GeV using the ATLAS detector, and the results are presented. Due to their high mass, these hypothetical particles would be very heavy and create noticeably slow-moving fragments in collisions. The search focused on slowly moving fragments with lower speed than the speed of light, specifically those with speed ratios as low as 0.03, in events involving high-energy proton collisions. The search used charged tracks created by energy loss as a sign to find these particles, and the results are presented for four hypothetical particle creations for masses up to 5.5 TeV, based on a predicted new type of particle called the "dark fermion." The results are also presented for stable, slow-moving versions of new particles created by other theories, and the results are used to set limits on these particles' existence. The results are used to set upper limits on these particles' existence based on new theories, and the results are used to set upper limits on these particles' existence based on new theories. The results are used to set limits on these particles' existence and the results are used to set limits on these particles' existence and the results are used to set limits on these particles' existence.

The research demonstrates an improvement in ridge waveguide designs for integration with photon sources, achieving high efficiency in photon generation. A finite-element method simulation of a ridge waveguide coupled to a quantum dot yielded a conversion efficiency of 98.4%  from electrical current to photons at the laser wavelength. This result indicates nearly perfect coherence in the photon emission process, meaning quantum interference only slightly affects photon release. By using a mode-matching approach to design the ridge waveguide, photon extraction was maximized. Furthermore, the study analyzes phenomena like Purcell enhancement and photon reabsorption in photon emission. Notably, Purcell enhancement exceeds 300 and photon reabsorption is minimized due to the ridge design. Additionally, the research considers heat transfer efficiency within the quantum dot, which was efficient despite the material's properties. This design holds potential for integration with quantum dots, enhancing their photon emission process.

In the context of high-temperature superconductivity, the 'boson summit' represents a collection of vibrational modes that could serve as the pairing glue for this phenomenon. Our research utilizes three inelastic neutron scattering experiments to thoroughly examine the boson summit's characteristics across various Ce$_{1-x}$La$_x$CuO$_{2+δ}$ samples, covering different temperatures and energy ranges. Through our findings, we discover that the boson summit exhibits an isotropic nature and non-isomorphic behavior with respect to the pseudogap and phonon regions, thus distinguishing it as a distinct spectral feature. Our analysis also reveals a correlation between this feature and oxygen disorder but not oxygen doping, and we conclude that the boson summit likely originates from a combination of low-frequency infrared modes and mid-range optical modes related to the lattice.

In theoretical particle physics, precise calculations are crucial for matching the exceptional accuracy of modern experimental measurements. This requires the ability to compute complex, higher-order multi-loop quantum corrections with extremely high precision. A significant challenge in this process is the evaluation of complicated integrals that arise in these calculations. Advances in computer algebra systems and the incorporation of exact mathematical expressions are enabling more accurate and efficient computations. This work delves into the accuracy of these complex integrals, particularly for cases involving multiple loops and scales, and is relevant in scenarios such as the top quark's anomalous magnetic moment and the three-loop contribution to the Cabbibo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix element.

We establish a set of summation rules for the average absorption probability of scattered waves when considering energy-dependent changes. This calculation is based on the overlap between a specific energy absorption operator and the scattering system's T matrix. By examining the energy absorption properties of scattered waves via the overlap of the absorption operator with the scattering system's T matrix, we derive energy-dependent summation rules for scattering amplitude-related quantities. This study extends previous work that focused on elastic scattering and includes analysis of the operator's connection to the scattering matrix and its underlying physical meaning. This connection reveals the existence of eigenchannels in the scattering process, for which we derive eigenchannel summation rules. These rules indicate that, on average, maximum absorption occurs when a scattering channel is completely closed.

Using archival data, we analyzed the 3-kpc spiral arm and discovered that it extends further into the galaxy than previously believed. The outer sections of this structure appear to be continuous with its inner parts. Utilizing gas tracers like Hα emission, CO, Fe, and Sn, we found the entire structure to be a single, albeit not uniform, feature. The entire structure has a mass of around 3.3 billion solar masses. The whole spiral arm structure is asymmetric, with a mass-to-luminosity ratio that decreases as it extends away from the galaxy's center. This variation supports the hypothesis that the spiral arm forms through a self-gravitating wave, with a coiling rate that slows down as it moves outward from the galaxy's center. This structure is more extensive in terms of radius, mass, and luminosity than any other spiral arm found in the galaxy.

In multi-objective optimization, a diverse range of non-dominating solutions is often highly desired. This study conducts a comprehensive analysis of a space known as phenotypic variety, which measures diversity among phenotypes resulting from different genetic assignments. We propose an assessment method based on the structure of multi-objective optimization's solution space and examine the effects of multi-objective and multi-algorithm interactions on phenotypic diversity. Our findings also investigate whether genetic diversity correlates with phenotypic diversity and whether phenotypic diversity influences phenotype quality.

This study examines the stable housemates dilemma by investigating whether distinct preferences among agents and numerous three-dimensional alternatives can yield unique outcomes. To commence, we demonstrate that both lexicographic and type-preference agents possess a unique solution in this specific scenario. Subsequently, with assumptions of either type-preference or distinct preferences, along with agents preferring their top significant alternative, we establish a multifaceted relationship between the diverse and type-based preference frameworks in terms of their generated stable matchings. Finally, based on these findings, we explore potential extensions beyond three-dimensional alternatives to different numbers of alternatives.

In-diamond growth directions affect valence band polar hole behavior by altering anisotropic spin splitting within the bands. This spin splitting is influenced by a specific electron-phonon interaction tied to long-range acoustic modes. We investigate this spin-splitting mechanism and its related electron-phonon coupling through calculations of polar valley Hall angles for various diamond growth influences. These results reveal that successful valley locking necessitates a very small Hall angle due to the rapid valley-degeneracy relaxation caused by an analogous phonon mechanism. Additionally, we assess how this valley-degeneracy relaxation mechanism impacts spin splitting within the bands.

The concept of clouds in the Gromov-Hausdorff category is defined, encompassing both centered and uncentered types. A rigorous definition of a cloud's center has been devised, facilitating a characterization of the entirety of a cloud within its own end. This approach resolves an issue that had been open for a significant period. As a practical application, a theoretical 'theorem of centroids' has been demonstrated, illustrating that nearly all 1-parameter families of compact metric spaces converge to a central element. Furthermore, an end-centered version of Gromov's filling radius definition has been formulated. This innovation enables a demonstration of the uniform convergences of sequences of Riemannian spheres under various scaling laws. Additionally, a notion of 'centered Gromov-Hausdorff convergence' has been proposed, facilitating the approximation of a target space by compact subspaces with specified properties. This innovation provides numerous advantageous properties. Finally, an innovative connection between Gromov-Hausdorff convergence and stochastic processes of Lévy-type escape has been established, connecting it to regenerative phenomena.

A significant limitation of conventional slot and microstrip antennas in wireless systems operating above 60 GHz is their narrow bandwidth. This study presents a novel wideband patch antenna design using magnetically resonant ground plane, facilitating broader bandwidth and precise beam control via magnetic resonance. The proposed antenna design mitigates the inherent radiating gap issue in traditional high-frequency patch antennas by incorporating an in-phase gap between magnetically resonant elements in the ground plane, enhancing both bandwidth and beam width.
