We discuss how these outcomes were measured experimentally and how they differ from theoretical predictions. We also explain that the extent of fusion beyond the predicted level varies with the number of particles in the outer shells of the colliding nuclei. We conclude by reporting recent advancements in understanding fusion behavior, including recent theoretical modeling using Trojan horse method.

The development and attributes of terrestrial planets are heavily influenced by their initial compositions. However, obtaining precise measurements of the compositions of star-forming regions remains a significant challenge. Researchers have therefore proposed an alternative strategy - using the chemical makeup of the host star as a proxy for the planet's core composition. This study aimed to assess the validity of this hypothesis by thoroughly analyzing star SPM J165542.43-444616.8, which is known to host a temperate super-Earth, S/Orb-1 b. The team employed various spectroscopic techniques to measure the abundances of 26 elements in the star, discovering an unusual deficiency in chromium, as well as distinctive sodium and lithium levels. Contrastingly, manganese showed a slight overabundance in line with other rocky exoplanets, and magnesium, aluminium, and silicon exhibited only amplitude deviations from solar values. The study concluded that Sodium and Chromium variations would significantly impact the rheology and convective patterns within the planet's interior, thereby influencing its geological and seismic characteristics.

Our proposal focuses on a location sensing system that uses low-frequency channels under a 5G/Wi-Fi band, as these channels are heavily affected by obstacles and can capture unique channel characteristics. We utilize a dataset collected in an office space and apply machine learning to analyze the signal and extract position-specific features. To address the irregular position distribution, we suggest employing an attention mechanism for efficient feature extraction and developing an algorithm to extract the most relevant features. Our results show that this approach enables accurate position tracking, and our method can be applied to existing Wi-Fi/5G devices for position estimation.

This paper proposes a comprehensive framework for the semantical integration of propositional modal logic by associating each world with a distinct semantic structure, similar to the way first-order logic is interpreted. The structure, known as an $\mathcal{L}^\Box$-model, consists of a base $\mathcal{L}$-model augmented with modal operators, where the accessibility of these operators is defined over the model's domain. This new semantic framework, rooted in categorical topology, offers a coherent approach to the study of modal logic. The paper also investigates fundamental properties of $\mathcal{L}^\Box$-models, including their projections, products, substructures, and homomorphisms, proving key results about their relationships to models of the underlying base logic. Specifically, projection and product operations preserve the logical equivalence between the two frameworks, while substructures and homomorphisms between $\mathcal{L}^\Box$-models can be used to define relations and functions between the relations accessibilities.

A bipartite graph's edges can be colored individually, whereas a painting involves assigning colors to vertices based on its edges. The concept of edge-coloring to produce a desired vertex color is referred to as edge-tinting. In 2008, Nakamura et al. discovered that every bipartite graph with no isolated vertices and a specific degree condition could edge-color a 3-edge color. Later, Li and Zhang proposed that this condition could be changed to 4, but it was eventually proven that this conjecture was incorrect. In this work, we believe that finding the precise edge-tinting number of some 4-regular bipartite graphs could help us better understand how to edge-color them.

We're examining functions defined over the vertices of an n-dimensional Hamming space, using values from a field of characteristic 2. Our focus lies on these functions' support sizes and their relationship with the function values when expanded using the Krawchuk basis up to a certain rank k. If the function values are limited to a maximum of M, we're interested in the function supports' minimum sizes under the condition that the function is zero at the vector 0 or has a derivative at the vector 0 of at most M. By analyzing the function on the Hamming space through its images under the Hamming group action, we've linked our problem to that of functions with nonnegative support sizes under the conditions mentioned above. Ultimately, our work provides a new proof of an existing theorem that gives the minimum support size of functions on the d-dimensional Hamming space with a nonnegative bound of M and a derivative at the vector 0 of at most M and a difference at the vector 0 of at most M.

COPASI is a comprehensive investigative tool for computational modeling in biology, enabling users to analyze, simulate, and explore complex models through both code and user-friendly interfaces. To accommodate user diversity, COPASI offers several R APIs, but crafting complex models can be time-consuming and require adjustments using its graphical user interface (GUI). When a model modification is necessary, inputting changes via the R interface may be the only option left, except for certain operations like level-3 constraints which can be managed through the R interface but lead to errors and demand time-consuming manual adjustments via the GUI. To address this limitation, a new tool, ShinyCOPASI, has been created as a web-based platform, enabling a seamless integration of COPASI's power with a modern, interactive interface, including level-3 constraints support, and thus, significantly improves workflow efficiency for researchers using COPASI.

This paper presents a comprehensive overview of uncertainty measurement in the field of AI for science, encompassing the challenges and principles associated with assessing uncertainty using machine learning models. It discusses various methods for creating and evaluating ambiguity assessments made by AI models, along with an analysis of their applicability to different areas of scientific research such as astronomy, biology, and physics. The study reveals a significant lack of consensus regarding the terminology, aims, and validation techniques for ambiguity assessment in scientific AI, prompting a need for further research and clarification. The paper also offers recommendations for future investigations and developments in this domain.

We investigate the von Neumann algebra generated by category functions within an arbitrary compact quantum group, demonstrating that this function is hermitian and belongs to the maximal torus subalgebra, while also establishing conditions under which it generates the entire subfactors. Additionally, the conditional expectation associated with this function has an explicit expression, and its fixed-point set can be explicitly identified. Furthermore, using this function, a new invariant for equivalence between compact quantum groups similar to a previously established invariant for finite groups has been introduced.

This study proposes a novel strategy iteration strategy that can deal with uncertainty in the Q-matrix. By introducing an interval for the probability of transition, the value iteration may not converge when this uncertainty is present. To address this issue, we formulate problem (3) as a linear complementarity problem (LCP) with different possible solutions. Our proposed strategy utilizes an approximate GMRES method to find a solution within the set of LCP's multiple solutions. We demonstrate that this approach ensures at least one solution exists and possesses optimality. A numerical example confirms the effectiveness of our proposed strategy in action.

Let Q be a weighted directed graph with n vertices and no repeated edges. The edge ideal of Q, denoted as I(Q), is a specific type of monomial ideal. Under certain conditions, such as having a quasisimple common subgraph, the Gabrielov number of I(Q) is equal to the Golod number of a related ideal I. These conclusions extend prior works by several authors in specific cases.

This paper introduces a novel multistep approach for tackling complex, computer-generated time series models through the Continuous Multidimensional Output Logarithmic Density estimator on multiple trajectories (COULDM) method. The technique evaluates the model's output at various time points and compares these values to observational data, addressing inference issues related to simulation output uncertainty and computational limitations. The method tackles the dual challenges of high-dimensional complexity and time-consuming simulations by assessing fewer, strategically selected time points. We examine its performance on artificial models in Python and emphasize a balanced consideration of accuracy and time efficiency. The COULDM method proves particularly effective, offering a versatile tool for analyzing complex, computer-generated time series models.

This study presents a novel approach to resilient learning by dividing the data into regional datasets and training separate models for each region. Each model is updated using only local data, reducing communication needs and preserving privacy. A key innovation is addressing data heterogeneity by preventing models from drifting from their respective regional distributions. A rigorous mathematical analysis confirms the approach's resilience to regional data variations and provides a clear condition for when this distributed method outperforms centralized training.

The characterization of the quark-gluon plasma is achieved by evaluating modifications to jets within the medium using high-statistics datasets from $\sqrt{s_\mathrm{NN}} =$ 5.02 TeV Pb-Pb and proton-proton collisions, captured by the CALOJET subsystem of the ATLAS detector. This analysis involves comparing fragmentation patterns of jets tagged by isolated photons and gluon candidates. Notably, although end-jet particles are moderately altered in Pb-Pb collisions, no notable disparities were found when contrasting tagged jets with lepton-tagged jets or non-tops events. Furthermore, simulations indicate that isolated photons retain integrity when traversing the quark-gluon medium, offering an effective guide to high-temperature regions.

Recent research involving Feynman integrals and Apéry numbers has led to the discovery of novel series with parity-based summation terms. Building upon recent findings, this paper reveals that the values of Apéry-like series, which feature specific weights and even/odd depths, directly correspond to intricate combinations of colored non-alternating multiple zeta expressions. These expressions, which were recently explored in a previous study, were found to be equivalent to key terms from Feynman graph expansions.

A brown dwarf located 47.5 parsecs away in the northern sky has an exceptionally low temperature of just 450 Kelvin. This object features a unique, bright polar cap, characterized by ammonia clouds that surround a cloudless area. Observations using the VLT/UVES spectrograph and a high-resolution map of the brown dwarf's surface reveal a distinct separation between the cool, ammonia-cloud-covered pole and the hotter, cloud-free area. The shape of the brown dwarf's orbit is not considered in these findings. The presence of convective storms is hypothesized to cause the separation of water and silicate materials, resulting in the brown dwarf's distinctive two-zone appearance.

The initial production of particles such as pions, kaons, protons, anti-protons and $\phi$-mesons is examined in Xe-Xe collisions at the LHC at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.44$ TeV using the ALICE detector. Our analysis focuses on these initial production stages in collisions involving no more than two particles. When compared to proton-proton collisions, there is no significant difference in the transverse momentum spectra of the various particles. However, when considering both particles and rapidity, distinct patterns emerge. In addition, our results show an increasing nuclear influence on these initial production stages with higher collision energies.

We have developed a novel, straightforward approach to interpolate parton distribution functions within their physical boundaries and extend them outside these limits using a simplified power-law formula. This method preserves key physical characteristics of the pDFs while accurately representing experimental data from a given scale down to a high-energy limit. Our approach outperforms the standard DGLAP evolution method, making it a versatile tool that can be applied to any set of pDFs with minimal inputs.

In-situ construction on other celestial bodies like the Moon and Mars is a key goal for establishing a long-term human presence. Using regolith and employing additive manufacturing could make this a reality, but first, we need to investigate the material's properties in greater detail. This study simulates regolith from Mars and the Moon through computer modeling, using finite element analysis and computational fluid dynamics to simulate SLS and EBM processes with varying heat levels and particle sizes. Results show that lower heat settings lead to more densely packed structures, with the formation of molten bridges between particles. Regolith formed under higher heat settings demonstrate an increase of up to 50% in compressive strength and hardness compared to those produced with lower heat. Moreover, higher heat settings result in a decrease of up to 50% in water absorption and higher relative density values of approximately 0.8.

The impact of surface slip on the Rayleigh-Plateau instability in a liquid layer is investigated. 
A theoretical model utilizing long-wave analysis is employed to derive and solve differential equations for both the slip and no-slip scenarios. 
By applying energy-based methods and analytical solutions for differential equations, it is found that a non-monotonic dispersion relation arises in the non-slip case, with a single critical wavelength determined by the Bond number. 
In the case of slip, a similar behavior is observed, but with an additional influence from the Beakham number, leading to various outcomes depending on the bond and beakham numbers, such as the non-existence of a critical wavelength, or the occurrence of two critical wavelengths, or only one critical wavelength in a limited range of the beakham number. 
Furthermore, the effects of surface slip on the critical wavelengths of the four distinct scenarios are analyzed using both theoretical and numerical methods, revealing a notable increase in the first critical wavelength, along with a significant decrease in the second critical wavelength.

We analyzed the photometric spectra of 19 local star-forming regions from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, finding H$\beta$ and [O III] $\lambda$5007 line emission. These findings were used to validate star formation rate (SFR) estimation methods and assess their accuracy, especially within the range of -1.5 < log$_{10}$(SFR) < -2.5 M$_{\odot}$/yr. In this lower SFR range, we found that estimating SFR based on H$\beta$ or [O III] emission can lead to incorrect values, typically underestimate SFR by about 0.5 dex. Furthermore, we observed that H$\beta$ tends to yield a more accurate SFR in lower star-forming regions, whereas [O III] tends to yield a more accurate SFR in higher regions. This discrepancy was attributed to [O III] emission's sensitivity to metallicity. Our [O III]-based SFR estimates showed a notable dependence on metallicity variations, particularly within the range 1.1 < log Z/Z$_{\odot}$ < 2.1, but H$\beta$ did not show such estimates, indicating it is more reliable for correcting metallicity-affected SFR calculations.

This research examines the Borel subalgebra of $\mathfrak{sl}_{N}$ and its associated fundamental regional modules, finding that their characteristics are captured by both their highest weights and certain cohomological properties of path spaces over the modules. A significant relationship is established between the structure of these path spaces and the quantum dimension calculations, leading to a comprehensive understanding of the module's underlying algebraic properties. A proportionality concept is developed within the context of these path spaces, providing insight into the modules' structure and revealing connections between regional modules that have the same highest weight. Ultimately, it is discovered that the modules and their associated path spaces exhibit symmetry, demonstrating invariance under the Weyl group actions and revealing connections between the modules and the fundamental weights, along with path space transformations that relate the modules and demonstrate a clear understanding of the module's underlying algebraic properties.

The diffusion process has become a prevalent solution for various invariance and data enhancement problems in the field of deep learning. In contrast to traditional methods that rely on adversarial training, our research presents DiffusionPath, an alternative approach that utilizes optimal control theory to solve the universal diffusion problem. We demonstrate that following the diffusion path uniquely resolves several critical problems, eliminating the need for sophisticated generative models. Additionally, our study resolves several challenging problems in diffusion generation, offering a straightforward solution for reverse diffusion through the direct minimization of a time-dependent cost function that explicitly depends on the data.

Handwritten mathematical expressions are written using motion data that can be captured from sensors. This method allows us to differentiate between complex equations, such as the quadratic formula, broken down into steps. However, recognizing equations written using ink is more challenging because it requires distinguishing between motion peaks corresponding to each step. This research presents a novel approach that leverages the advantages of both sensor-driven and ink-based handwriting. By incorporating noise robustness into the process, the complexity of the equation can be identified accurately, and each step can be understood individually for further analysis.

To accelerate the development of speech recognition systems, we propose a quicker approach for generating synthetic speech. Traditionally, non-statistical methods are utilized for speech length simulation, but they fall short in accurately mimicking the length distribution. We present a median-based strategy for quickly simulating speech duration, and evaluate both the efficiency of this method and its effectiveness in matching the actual distribution of speech lengths.

Conservation strategies rely on accurate assessment of species' presence within their habitats. However, traditional methods often struggle to accurately detect rare species or account for measurement inaccuracies during surveys. Improved spatial modeling, which combines precision and practicality, can help bridge this gap but are not yet widely used in practice. A novel family of spatial models, known as integrated density models, has potential to provide highly precise detection while keeping the models simple and easy to operate. These models can be applied to various species combinations and are now made easier to implement with a corresponding R package, 'spHabitat', that allows users to fit spatial models and create visual representations of species distributions. This research evaluates various model combinations using realistic data to compare their effectiveness and presents case studies demonstrating the use of these models with existing data for a bird species.

Skin cancer holds the highest incidence rate among all cancer types in the US.
Teaching medical professionals to accurately recognize skin abnormalities is a
critical component of medical education. The traditional visual learning methods
used in dermatology education are increasingly being supplemented by interactive
tech-based approaches centered on automated diagnosis of skin conditions.
One such system, The Skincare Initiative (TSI), combines a vast digital library
of skin images with an AI-driven diagnosis tool capable of identifying benign
moles and aggressive skin conditions such as dysplastic moles and skin cancers.
Using image data corresponding to healthy skin patterns, TSI employs an interactive
protocol to analyze skin images and determine whether they exhibit irregular
patterns or require further examination. Users can also interact with TSI by
manually highlighting and comparing moles to the reference database, enabling
the system to learn and refine its diagnosis capabilities over time through a
customized training process. Technical documentation providing details on TSI's
architecture and design is available for reference.

To predict a SNIA's distance more accurately by analyzing its spectral sequence, we need to reduce the uncertainty in our predictions. Currently, researchers manually select important spectral features, but this approach is not ideal. Therefore, we need to develop a model that automatically identifies significant spectral features and minimizes uncertainty, making it suitable for handling sequential data. A probabilistic autoencoder was applied to SNIA sequences, and when combined with traditional distance metrics, it outperformed other models in both feature selection and predictive performance, as shown by its lower redshift root mean square error and coefficient of variation. Furthermore, our study reveals the significance of spectral features in the 5500-6500 Angstrom range for determining distances, supporting the creation of more precise photometric models for future wide-field surveys.

A massive galaxy cluster acting as a gravitational lens has amplified and distorted the light from a distant star-forming galaxy at z=2.09. High-resolution images from the Atacama Telescope have identified a small star-forming region in the galaxy, which is likely driven by a massive stellar source. This low-density outflow carries little mass but moves at significant speeds, possibly exceeding the escape velocity of the galaxy. While a part of the outflow may escape the galaxy, it is predominantly confined by the dense interstellar medium. Using a simulated model, researchers have found that a unique type of outflow could effectively heat and ionize the surrounding dust in the galaxy, effectively reconciling conflicting measurements of dust temperature.

The growth dynamics of turbulent plumes are fundamentally altered by a solid boundary, leading to intricate flow patterns and dynamic behavior in plume expansion. We investigate and differentiate between two key incorporation mechanisms by which particles are integrated into these plumes: one characterized by gradual increases in incorporation rate over time, and the other by rapid increases in incorporation rate followed by a decline. Our study reveals that this character of turbulent plume expansion can be integrated into a cohesive framework through the concept of effective viscosity, which is influenced by the Strahler number of the plume and can vary significantly in magnitude, contributing to diverse plume expansion behaviors.

Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, or interdependent systems, can provide critical insights into potential outbreaks. Traditionally, networks have been modeled as collections of connections between individuals and infected groups. However, another form of interaction exists - that of multiple individuals interacting together, known as multibody interactions. These interactions can be explored through the study of multibody interactions and hypergraphs, where each group of connected individuals represents a clique of nodes.

Researchers have developed theoretical frameworks that allow for the analysis of complex networks, or epidemics on these networks, using spectral limits. These spectral limits help provide an approximate threshold for when an epidemic will or won't spread, using the eigenvalues and vectors of the network's adjacency matrix. Previous research had shown that, under the assumption of homogeneous networks, this threshold can be calculated exactly, but this left a gap in knowledge regarding the exact eigenvalue threshold.

Recent research has closed this gap, showing that the spectral threshold indeed serves as the final decision-making factor in determining whether the epidemic will or won't spread, even when groups of connected individuals vary in size and the underlying network structure is irregular. Moreover, a new algorithm has been created that can estimate this threshold more accurately using a sub-linear time method, making epic predictions more feasible and realistic.

Recent studies discovered that certain 2D crystals exhibit magnetic properties when their torsional symmetry is altered by a certain degree. By altering the R-angle between adjacent layers in multilayered CrI3 crystals, researchers found that this variation impacts the spin-network within the crystal in an otherwise two-dimensional ferromagnet. According to theoretical calculations and experimental data from magnetic resonance imaging and neutron scattering, it has been confirmed that this spin-pattern can be described as a linear combination of two distinct patterns: one influenced by chirality and the other by magnetic properties. Furthermore, additional evidence suggests that a dimensionless parameter that influences the relative-contribution of these two patterns can be controlled by altering fundamental crystal characteristics, such as atomic size, bond strength and lattice spacing.

Through the utilization of magnetic cycle simulations, we examine the impact of rotation profiles, adopting either the $\Omega-$ or $\Omega_{\rm{eff}}-$ $\Omega-$ effects, on the potential cycles, employing Miesch's rotation profile as a case study. Our results demonstrate the significant influence of differential rotation, particularly its $\Omega-$ $\Omega_{\rm{eff}}-$ characteristics, on both the onset and period of these cycles. Furthermore, we have established a method for mapping rotation profiles, based on Reynolds-Olson diagnostic, to predict the presence of magnetic cycles, thus enabling to eliminate or diminish certain previously reported potential cycles from slowly rotating stars. Interestingly, adjustments in the super-ionic layer can have the效果 to induce magnetic cycles in very slowly rotating stars like AD Leo. Our study also considers scenarios where the $\Omega-$ $\Omega_{\rm{eff}}-$ effects play a pivotal role in driving magnetic cycles, even considering scenarios where the shear itself might not directly contribute to the dynamo process.

Deep multimodal learning through the integration of multiple information sources is a crucial area of research. This study presents a deep framework called K-fan, which simultaneously processes multiple types of data such as text, images, audio, and more. Several key aspects differentiate K-fan from traditional single-task models and sequential approaches: its ability to learn a shared representation space, efficiently handle information leakage, and learn relationships between different data modalities. This is achieved through multiple innovations, including a shared multimodal representation module, individual modalities-specific leakage control units, and hierarchical correlation analysis. This study thoroughly evaluates K-fan on three diverse datasets, highlighting its superiority over competing methods. Additionally, it contributes significantly to the learning theory by examining the sample complexity of high-dimensional deep networks in the presence of modalities.

Initial research on the validity of multi-threaded programs used model checkers that employed DPOR to generate precise, non-overlapping execution sequences. These early checkers significantly contributed to the understanding of program correctness by ensuring that equal programs produced the same outcomes. However, as they struggled with complexity in more intricate programs, it became evident that optimizing DPOR was a necessary step forward. This paper introduces McMini, a adaptable DPOR-based model checker designed to analyze multi-threaded programs. McMini supports a comprehensive array of synchronization types and handles various programming languages such as C, Java, and Python. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of McMini in testing various DPOR strategies while achieving notable performance improvements, outperforming the current top-model checker for this type of analysis.

In recent years, the widespread adoption of WhatsApp has led to a growing concern over its role in disseminating misinformation. Although the organization behind WhatsApp has recognized this issue and implemented measures to curb its spread, such as limiting forwardings, the effectiveness of these measures remains untested. Our study aimed to investigate whether restricting user abilities to share content without verification in WhatsApp metadata can diminish the propagation of misinformation. We conducted an empirical investigation by creating two versions of the popular 2016 US Presidential Election Fake News dataset, incorporating both true and false articles, and distributing them to US participants in the form of an online survey. Notably, one group of participants had access to features that tracked the origin and spread of each shared message, mimicking WhatsApp's message tracking, while the other group used a control version of the platform with no such features. Our results showed that individuals who were prevented from freely sharing content experienced a significant decrease in the likelihood of sharing misinformation, especially when they were able to see the message path, indicating a 30-40% reduction. Conversely, participants who were allowed to share content without limits exhibited little to no reduction in the sharing of misinformation. Furthermore, the effects observed were more pronounced among those who were less tech-savvy, despite our study efforts to replicate a natural understanding of the task. We discuss the broader implications of these findings, as well as the limitations and potential future research directions.

We analyze a random population model where individuals reproduce independently, creating a large number of offspring, following a distribution that varies by individual. A sample of individuals is drawn from this population, and the frequency of each allele within the sample is examined. Our results show that, as the population size approaches infinity, the distribution of alleles in this population follows a specific pattern, and the precise shape of this pattern depends on the diversity of allele variations within the population. Our findings also reveal how the prevalence of rare alleles in this population is influenced by a parameter related to population genetics.

This paper proposes an Attended Activation Mechanism (AM) designed to enhance the detection capabilities of speech spoofing counteraction systems. We begin by describing a baseline end-to-end spoofing detection model, and then illustrate how our mechanism can be integrated into such a system. Through comprehensive experiments conducted on the ASV-SPoojering 2019 evaluation platform, using a diverse set of 1888 sentences and five distinct spoofing generators, we demonstrate that AM can be applied across a range of spoofers and significantly improve the accuracy of speech authentication tasks. Notably, our method achieves a maximum performance gain of 47% over the baseline model.

We've developed a new class of supersymmetric inflation models with superior
properties. In traditional local supersymmetric models, making the Goldstino
move rapidly in field space results in an excessively complex non-minimal
coupling to the inflaton, rendering the models invalid. However, our new local
models exhibit relatively simple non-gravitational, non-minimally coupled terms.
Additionally, our enhanced models incorporate substantial supergravity contributions
during inflation, thereby reducing fine-tuning requirements. From a broader
perspective, these refined local models demonstrate that supergravity's impact
during inflation can be advantageous, even facilitating a more accurate description.

When associated with a symmetry group in group theory, it makes sense, but when it comes to geometry, the term takes on a different meaning where symmetrical objects are generally considered balanced. In this study, we examine the balance of two methods, namely, difference operators and inverse values, which rely on whether two elements can be transformed into each other through rotation or reflection. We apply this approach to photon pairs generated through parametric down-conversion and demonstrate that the concept of symmetry can yield unexpected outcomes based on how we define it. Moreover, the concept of balance can also depend on whether it involves reflection processes, and as expected, more complex systems where multiple pairs are produced may exhibit balancing effects across different factors where they are not visible in simpler setups involving single particles.

Our investigation employs terahertz near-field scanning interference microscopy to investigate samples of superconducting quantum circuits in the microwave frequency range. The scanning terahertz electric field probe enables us to map the wave function of a处于共振状态的超导量子谐振器 with remarkable spatial and spectral precision. Our findings confirm that this probe is capable of detecting coherent quantum states with an average photon number of one, and it can effectively measure wave function properties of a处于非共振状态的量子谐振器. Our research substantiates the capability of scanning terahertz probes for probing samples that are based of microwave resonators. Our scanning terahertz probe operates independently of a specific measurement methodology, rendering scanning terahertz microscopy a versatile tool for exploring a wide range of quantum and classical electromagnetic systems, particularly when they are in close physical proximity.

We investigate how to partition the real line into uncountably many sets, focusing on specific types such as Borel, analytic sets, and Lebesgue measurable sets. It is established that certain partitioning schemes are equivalent when certain set properties are used. We establish a partitioning scheme for Borel sets and demonstrate its independence from ZFC. However, a new model of ZFC shows that using a Sierpinski tree results in a partition where each set contains a non-measurable subset. We establish that certain properties of partitionings are closed under taking subcollections and established the containment of a Sierpinski partition within a partitioning scheme of Pol spaces of countable order. This, in turn, implies that each set in these partitioning schemes contains a L\'{u}byn set.

In recent years, there has been significant growth in the use of agent-based models for simulating and analyzing financial markets. Building on existing agent-based models, our research introduces an innovative approach, presenting two new strategies. We apply our models to simulate a new, large investment fund and examine the impact on their returns. Our results show that the behavior of such strategies enables them to profit from the behaviors of other, more conventional investment approaches. However, it appears their profits come primarily at the expense of individual traders rather than institutional investors. We examine the potential consequences for the development of new agent-based models in the field.

Researchers employing active protocols identification methods send diverse, random protocols in the form of packets to a network interface and analyze the responses in order to determine the network's services. These techniques are employed by attackers as well for service discovery purposes. Our investigation utilizes random approach-based tools, such as NetCat and splay, which utilize random flags, ports, and setup requests, but without utilizing system calls. These tools have a limited ability to identify services and have an inherent time constraint. Nevertheless, they can be optimized to improve their effectiveness and efficiency. Our research demonstrates that this can be achieved by modifying the tools to increase their packet interarrival times and utilize existing tools features more effectively. These optimizations can result in reduced tool resource usage and increased service discovery time, making a potential vulnerability on the network's part. Nevertheless, such optimizations render the assault more realistic and provide an understanding of the effectiveness and efficiency of active protocols identification methods.

We investigate the dynamic properties of a magnon superconductor gateway built with a thin PYNi5 multilayer. In the presence of a superconducting layer, the gateway allows magnon signals to be isolated when the superconductor enters the paired state, not when it's in the normal state. This response is evident in both transmitted and reflected magnon peaks. Additionally, we observe a significant and unexpected increase in magnon gating based on their frequency, specifically, lower-frequency magnons exhibit better isolation in comparison to higher-frequency counterparts.

A significant obstacle in developing powerful general-purpose audio recognition systems is the labor-intensive process of creating large, diverse audio-visual datasets. This task becomes even more complex given the vast number of possible sound categories. Recent attempts to address this issue have led to the creation of data-rich environments for learning, where new categories can be learned without prior examples. Our work focuses on creating a new challenge in audio recognition by having contributors add new sound categories unknown to the system, highlighting the difficulty in handling diverse and evolving datasets in real-world scenarios. This is particularly relevant in the context of federated learning, a decentralized machine learning approach that allows multiple devices to collaborate in training without sharing sensitive data. By implementing a novel framework for federated learning with new categories, we demonstrate the challenges and limitations of current methods, and propose potential solutions for creating collaborative and dynamic audio recognition systems.

There is a need for an efficient method to verify Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states across multiple dimensions. The GHZ-state evaluation index, a novel index designed for this purpose, uses specific correlations to verify the properties of quantum systems. Through theoretical analysis and numerical experiments, it's shown that this index can accurately verify quantum systems in both deterministic and probabilistic scenarios. The index relies on a specific relationship between quantum systems in different dimensions, using a set of operators with distinct algebraic characteristics to maximize correlation. Furthermore, this research outlines a comprehensive strategy to verify high-dimensional quantum systems as the number of particles increases. The index requires fewer measurement instances compared to traditional methods, making it a more practical and scalable solution as quantum technologies continue to advance.

A wireless system architecture that incorporates a configurable, intelligently placed array of passive reflectors has shown significant promise in enhancing the performance of weak wireless connections. However, the large number of elements in these arrays poses a significant challenge for accurate estimation of the direct and reflected signal paths. In an effort to alleviate this burden, a novel two-step estimation technique has been introduced that leverages the similarities between these channels and significantly reduces the overhead associated with communication. In the context of time-division-duplex systems, this technique first obtains the reflected path by exploiting the correlation between pilot signals and then utilizes it to recover the direct path. In order to minimize estimation errors, a closed-form expression was derived for the minimum number of pilot symbols needed to achieve a predetermined level of accuracy. When extended to multiple users with orthogonal access, this framework demonstrates considerable advantages over traditional approaches in terms of reduced overhead and improved performance.

This research examines how U.S. regional news outlets reported on the U.S. COVID pandemic from March 1, 2020, to March 1, 2021, analyzing both the volume and direction of coverage in relation to cases, death rates, and population from the most affected states and deaths and death rates at a national level. Utilizing UT Austin's Common Crawl Archive and an NLP approach, we user-defined key terms for the pandemic and calculated the volume and direction of coverage using an HPS model. Our investigation discovered a unit root, indicating media influence on public perception, as well as varying levels of negativity or positivity in reporting, which was associated with shifts in cases and death rates. Additionally, we investigated audience size changes in response to pandemic death rates. Using time-lagged variables in our analysis revealed responses in both public perception and audience size following increases or decreases in death rates.

The fundamental skill of counting, a key milestone in childhood development, has been a challenging aspect to explore due to its short duration. Recent advancements in deep learning now enable researchers to study the development of basic cognitive abilities over extended periods. This study investigates the skill acquisition of counting using agents trained in a learned counting task using deep reinforcement learning. To overcome a common limitation of deep reinforcement learning, where skills are typically static, we've implemented counting tasks that continue over extended time frames. The experiment reveals that when standard neural networks are used for learning to count, they're prone to cheating. However, the incorporation of the biological phenomenon of recurrent weights in neural networks prevents cheating. Furthermore, the same effect can be achieved by introducing a mechanism for long-term memory. This effect can be quantified using the QAPoC score and the time it takes for agents to resist cheating. Our findings also show an analogy between the emergence of accurate counting in the model and the human acquisition of cardinality representation.

A variation of a Bloom filter called a xor filter offers a compromise between space efficiency and query speed, by utilizing word-level disjunction with bitwise XOR operations instead of the usual OR operations. A fundamental theorem underpins xor filters and enables their construction. Moreover, a two-stage xor filter can significantly shorten average query times to near constant values. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of xor filters compared to other adaptive structures, showing that they offer comparable or better performance terms of space efficiency and query speed. Additionally, xor filters provide constant-time membership queries with low but non-zero false positive rates. Furthermore, xor filters exhibit superior performance in terms of usage speed and memory usage. Finally, xor filters support dynamic operations such as insert and delete, which can be executed efficiently.

This paper draws connections between various branches of mathematics, 
specifically between the properties of entire functions and convex sets in
the complex plane. Several key relationships between these fields are explored.
In addition to a Weierstrass-type theorem for Finsler metrics, the paper 
includes metric spaces with properties of finite dimension, as well as a result 
describing the structure of plurisubharmonic functions. Furthermore, a section 
of the paper covers sublinear expectations and random convex bodies.

This study offers an advanced methodology for forecasting market trends, analyzing market transactions based on timing, expense, and quantity to uncover hidden patterns in market trends. For this purpose, We created a Tagged Continuous Conditional Random Tagging Model that simultaneously forecasts market trends and pinpoints vital patterns within it. This model offers tag accuracy advantages over existing techniques by effectively managing temporal dependencies among tags and offering tagged subsequences that capture essential information about future market trends. This model's effectiveness was verified through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on a dataset consisting of real stock transactions, demonstrating its output superiority across multiple evaluation criteria to accurately predict market trends. On examination, our model demonstrated to be feature-rich and interpretable by successfully categorizing both short and long-lasting market trends while predicting their cessation times with considerable accuracy. This capability enables investors to make well-informed trading decisions.

Federated Learning (FL) has become an essential technique for preserving user
privacy in distributed machine learning and has achieved significant success in
various real-world applications in the mobile and internet sectors. Although
utilizing local data increases data's anonymity, it's susceptible to attacks
targeting participation, indicating, and stored data. To address this vulnerability,
we introduce a novel FL approach called FLVoogd inspired by differential privacy,
aiming to block malicious activities and mitigate data leakage. This framework
incorpor a local FL model training phase with differential privacy additions and
an aggregated server model that employs a Gaussian mixture model to filter out
FlVoogd: Resilient And Privacy Retaining Federated Learning 3
anomalies. Through simulations on different datasets, we demonstrate that FLVoogd
can effectively resist various attacks while retaining user privacy.

Achieving a balance between robustness and adaptability in end-to-end autonomous driving systems is a significant challenge due to the gap between simulated and real-world environments. Most training algorithms become rigid once trained, rendering them incapable of adapting to unforeseen circumstances. To address this issue, we've devised a two-pronged approach that utilizes two distinct modules - one to bridge the simulation-reality gap by adapting weights trained in different environments, and the other to dynamically adjust the system's objective function based on real-time performance feedback. We evaluate our framework using a complex driving scenario that involves navigating an unsignalized intersection, and use it to assess the robustness and adaptability of our architecture through various real-world driving conditions. The extensive dataset comprises 1323 frames and demonstrates that our controller can effectively handle perturbations and adapt to various situations.

The deepfake phenomenon has become a pressing concern in various sectors, including journalism and politics, due to its potential to be misused. In response to this issue, our team proposes a novel deepfake creation method, referred to as DeepCover, capable of seamlessly integrating fabricated content into strong facial identities under challenging conditions. DeepCover is distinguished by its ability to accommodate content on diverse scales and orientations, effectively addressing weak boundaries and transfer marks often associated with existing deepfake creation techniques. Furthermore, our single-stage framework seamlessly combines facial replacement, style transfer, and refinement, resulting in high-quality deepfakes with minimal computational resources. Consequently, our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art deepfake creation approaches in terms of its ability to deceive existing deepfake detectors and visual evaluation metrics. To further push the boundaries of deepfake creation, we then integrate DeepCover into large image-to-image transformation models, yielding even more sophisticated and robust deepfakes. To address the issue of deepfake identification, we introduce a novel identification approach, which leverages the knowledge from numerous unlabelled samples to detect deepfakes with extremely low resource requirements. Thorough evaluations on various public and private datasets demonstrate the exceptional performance of DeepCover in creating state-of-the-art robust deepfakes and our proposed identification approach in terms of accuracy, precision, and robustness.

The existence of supercritical fluids like dissolved gases, which may be present in the atmospheres of certain exoplanets, has yet to be confirmed. However, their presence in the atmospheres of massive gas giants in our solar system can be accurately modeled. By applying similar logic to temperate sub-Neptunes that are significantly smaller, our research suggests that some of these planets may actually harbor concealed oceans in a state of supercriticality. These concealed oceans could potentially be super-critical as well, especially if the planet is located closer to its star. Our findings indicate that the ultimate fate of a planet's atmosphere depends on whether a particular balance is achieved between heat and gas. Specifically, for many temperate sub-Neptunes, their atmospheres could contain a distinct "clearing layer" where light easily passes through because gas does not absorb light as much as aerosols do. This effect, of clearing the atmosphere and making it more transparent, could potentially mask a signature indicating temperatures within the atmosphere. Since it is believed that most temperate sub-Neptunes are composed of water, we propose that the water present in these planets has condensed, and that their atmospheres contain an opaque "final skin" made of a super-critical ocean and mineral sediments. Our research suggests that the concealed ocean may originate from cryogenic ices that migrated from the planet's interior and that their atmospheres contain an opaque "final skin" made of a super-critical ocean and mineral sed

Achieving complex pattern recognition in neural networks requires a network architecture that can learn through learning rules inspired by biological processes. Our research introduces a new learning rule for recognizing intricate patterns, drawing inspiration from the visual cortex of the brain and utilizing a type of neural network based on real-time information exchange. Through our simulation using artificial patterns, we demonstrated that our proposed learning rule can effectively facilitate the formation of feature detectors essential for recognizing complex patterns at an early stage of visual processing.

This report presents a detailed analysis of our team's submission to the Out-of-Lexicon Challenge. Our approach involved generating semantic representations for input sentences using a combination of Bayesian neural networks and autoencoders. This enabled us to explore and capture complex sentence structures and meanings beyond a predefined vocabulary.

A new approach combines the generalized polynomial chaos expansion method with the finite element method to solve complex problems involving uncertainty in scientific computations. We've developed a non-intrusive post-Apriori estimation technique to assess the accuracy of this expansion by controlling its truncation error. Our approach divides the total error into identifiable components and bounds the irreducible part of the error. Furthermore, we've adapted the adaptive finite element method for our framework, targeting the efficient resolution of nonlinear elasticity problems with multiple sources of randomness. Our algorithm identifies and refines errors related to the mesh and the polynomial expansion, ultimately achieving an optimal balance between computational effort and accuracy.

This paper addresses the challenge of detecting and isolating changes in a system where not all variables can be observed, some of which are hidden. Specifically, it focuses on scenarios with single input and single output, and all other variables can be divided into two groups: visible and invisible. The paper presents an algorithm that uses the difference between expected and actual output to identify and isolate only the changes affecting the invisible variables. These changes include sudden shifts, gradual changes, and forces applied to the system. Once the algorithm identifies these anomalies, it switches the system to a control mode that can adapt to the new conditions. Specifically, it calculates the difference between expected and actual partial system output using the invisible variables as a basis for correction and control. The paper proposes a method based on Riccati difference equations to calculate and adjust this difference, and then develops a model predictive control algorithm to optimize the system's performance and ensure its stability. Finally, it demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm through numerical simulations of the system's behavior.

We analyze the formation and evolution of satellite dwarf galaxies using the 100m Nancay Radiotelescope's deep HI surveys, supplemented by archival HST data, and existing chemical abundance studies. These galaxies existed before the formation of the Milky Way's disk, making their existence before the acquisition of the Sagittarius system the oldest structure in the Galaxy. Their exploration helps us understand the building blocks of the Milky Way before the formation of its light.

Given a continuous action of a profinite group $\Gamma$ on a space $X$, we construct an action spectrum $\Sigma^{vir}_{\Gamma,X}$, which is the space of homotopy orbits $X_{\Gamma}$. We then demonstrate that this action spectrum carries a action of the loop space $\mathcal{L}\Gamma$ via a map from the fibration spectrum $\mathcal{L}\Gamma \wr \Sigma^{vir}_{\Gamma,X}$ to $\Sigma^{vir}_{\Gamma,X}$, for an object $X$ in $\mathop{\bf Spectra}^{\Gamma}$. Moreover, we show that the virtual equivariant cohomology $\mathop{\bf Cohomology}^{eq}(\mathop{\bf Spectra})$ provides a representation of such action spectra. Additionally, we use this concept to prove a generalized form of the Petersen-Wedge Theorem for loop space profinite groups.

Training state-of-the-art models for visually complex documents demands a substantial number of labeled examples, which often exceeds available training data. To work around this limitation, training on larger datasets leads to improved model performance and reduced dependency on labeling costs. This effect is particularly pronounced for models leveraging frameworks like LayoutLMv2 and Donut. We discovered that increasing the training dataset to just 150% significantly boosts efficiency and minimizes extraction errors. These findings facilitate a much cheaper approach to document structure-aware extraction tasks, including forms and invoices.

Our investigation of EuS/InAs heterostructures has utilized an advanced combination of analysis techniques to examine the electronic structure and spin-dependent properties of the interface in great detail. Utilizing M\"{o}bius strip configuration to ensure a defect-free interface, we employed X-ray and ultraviolet photoemission spectroscopy to analyze spin-split valence bands. Our results indicate that the spin-dependent properties of the interface originate from InAs, exhibiting a $0.2\ eV$ spin splitting which grows to $0.5\ eV$ after annealing, accompanied by the emergence of interface states at a binding energy of $0.3\ eV$. Furthermore, the density of these interface states shows distinct spin texture characteristics, exhibiting an odd parity in spin orientation relative to the momentum, consistent with the influence of strong magnetic anisotropy from EuS. Our study sheds light on the complex interaction between the two materials and paves the way for investigating 2D magnetic phenomena.

A significant result by Wadge demonstrated that continuous functions can induce a well-ordered structure on the power set of the Baire space by partitioning it into equivalence classes based on reducibility. It has since been established that each of these classes can be represented as the preimage of a Borel set under every continuous function. The purpose of this research is to develop a efficient algorithm that assigns to every Borel set its specific position in this well-ordered structure.

Highly efficient deep neural network (DNN) models have become increasingly critical in empowering a wide range of internet applications and services. Pruning has emerged as a leading approach to optimizing DNN models for enhanced efficiency. Current research predominantly relies on reducing the number of connections within a model, which often compromises its predictive accuracy. Our investigation focuses on fine detailed architectures of models and their associated weight matrices. Surprisingly, our research reveals that reducing the number of rows within these weight matrices yields superior performance compared to traditional methods that focus on columns. This discovery leads to the creation of ClickTrain, an innovative and generalizable click-based pruning algorithm applied to both 2D and 3D layer types. ClickTrain outperforms existing algorithms across a wide range of common models and their corresponding base models. Furthermore, our research introduces two innovative strategies to improve the computational speed and memory usage of models without sacrificing their overall prediction precision and accuracy. ClickTrain excels in producing high-performance models with significantly elevated operational efficiency. It provides a substantial 3.17x-fx6.x times improvement in model compression compared to the existing best results and maintains a high level of accuracy even when compressing models heavily.

This study expands the modality in the Lambek Calculus by defining new structural rules that govern the interaction between modal operators and the tensor product (concatenation) as well as the par operation.  It has been proven that these modal rules are equivalent to the application of modalities on the tensor product and the par operation in a way that preserves completeness within the context of non-associative linear logic frameworks.  We specifically focus on a subset of the logic, known as the distributive complete Lambek Calculus, and demonstrate its relationship to a specific type of semiring that is closed under certain operations.  The inclusion of modal operators does not compromise this relationship, and it is subsequently applied to a subset of this logic, called the distributive sub-logic, and shown to have a specific connection to a type of semiring that is closed under three binary operations.

The observation of neutron star - black hole mergers through gravitational waves offers a singular opportunity to study matter under extreme conditions and black hole populations. Gravitational wave signals produced by these events are complicated by the neutron star's neutron fluid, resulting in the distinctive modification of tidal parameters. A collaborative effort involving Oxford University and the University of the Western Cape seeks to establish an adaptable machine learning framework for classifying such events, which can operate efficiently on existing and upcoming gravitational wave detectors such as LIGO, Virgo, and the space-based detector future.

Our analysis of the Kepler observations reveals a transiting exoplanet, designated TOI-5542b, with well-defined characteristics: a radius of approximately 1.09 Jupiter radii, a mass of about 1.32 times that of the Sun, and an estimated orbital period of around 282 days. The planet's low density suggests a composition consistent with a large gas giant, and its long orbital period implies a cold atmosphere. Notably, TOI-5542 is an ancient, metal-deficient star, making the discovery of this gas giant intriguing, as gas giant planets are typically not found around metal-deficient stars. The planet, a hot Jupiter, has a relatively wide orbit, implying that it likely migrated inward after forming. The discovery of this gas giant on a wide orbital path presents a unique opportunity to study its atmospheric properties and the dynamics of its low-metal environment.

In a Restricted Markov Decision Process, a key constraint limits which transitions can occur from a set of permitted, "safe" states. To tackle this issue, a regularization technique was developed that utilizes the Lagrange dual function to generate useful gradients for solving PRMDPs. Since obtaining the dual function directly can be challenging, a novel approximation was created by leveraging subgradients of the dual function, derived from solving closely related PRMDPs with slight variations. This work outlines a non-smooth optimization approach utilizing these approximations and proves convergence under specific, generally applicable conditions. Additionally, a simpler PRMDP variant, known as the Symmetric Restricted Markov Decision Process, was designed for easier computation of subgradients. Numerical experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of this method in solving both PRMDPs and SSRMDPs.

This research offers a comprehensive survey of online recognition methods for handwritten mathematical expressions, beginning with an overview of essential background information on neural networks, crude character recognition, and the segmentation of text. It then delves into three primary online recognition strategies: the application of continuous convolutional neural networks (CNN) generalizations, the utilization of convolutional neural networks in conjunction with recurrent neural networks (RNN), and a variation of free-transform recognition that employs CNNs and hybrid recognition methods. The background information on mathematical expressions and the comparison between online and offline recognition are also presented.

We observe that a linear combination of the H^1 and H^0 sheaf cohomology groups from a line bundle over a Riemann surface can represent the quantum dynamics in a superconformal chiral 2d N=2 theory. Specifically, the time-dependent state vector's evolution corresponds to a section of the total space of this bundle, where the cohomology section's CS equation is derived from the theory's equation of motion. We also establish a connection between the cohomology group's structure and the S-matrix, and demonstrate how the H^1 cohomology group's sections, representing 1-cycles on the surface, map to the resonant states of the theory. Furthermore, these 1-cycles can correspond to the anyonic states of the 2d N=2 SUSY quantum Hall effect.

This study examines the dynamics of interaction propagation within networks utilizing a novel approach to measure the behavior of random network models. Our analysis reveals that the system's variations, assessed through the H-entropy of node state distributions, consistently exhibit a two-component pattern across different network types, comprising high-frequency minor fluctuations and low-frequency significant changes. To further investigate this phenomenon, we introduce the concept of network variance and analyze its relationship with the network structure. Our results show that nodes located near high-variability time intervals have a significantly elevated likelihood of being pivotal network elements with broad coverage. These findings provide a novel perspective on the concept of network instability.

Our enhanced Actor-Critic (EAC) approach rectifies issues with traditional actor-critic methods in reinforcement learning (RL), which can be unstable when using parametric function approximators to model the policy and value functions. Traditional actor-critic methods typically approximate the policy using maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) based on the current value function. However, this our EAC method employs Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) in place, generating a more robust sample from the policy's true distribution and thereby producing higher-quality action samples for the critic. Furthermore, the HMC method enables exploration of the entire distribution, allowing the agent to discover unexpected yet potentially highly rewarding areas in the state-action landscape. The effectiveness of the EAC method is demonstrated by superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines, as well as reduced variance in learning when testing RL tasks.
A fundamental proof of the well-known twin prime hypothesis is provided.

Recent advancements in stratified navigation techniques have demonstrated remarkable success in resolving complex real-world challenges. Despite these developments, practical applications are still hindered due to difficulties in coordinating multiple complex sensors and processing substantial data sets in real-time. Our research focuses on overcoming these challenges by developing a robust and efficient robot perception system centered on Sonar integration. This system leverages the Sonar's unique capability to provide and update 360-degree spatial information sequentially. Our findings show that Sonar, specifically the Hitachi HUC-04 model, offers a cost-effective and highly reliable solution for robot navigation by delivering a balanced combination of performance and resource efficiency. Our work details the detailed integration of Sonar with underlying control mechanisms and presents a general framework applicable to any hybrid navigation system. This framework can be utilized by any system incorporating Sonar to enhance their hybrid navigation capabilities. Our results are sonar-specific and can serve as a foundational blueprint for similar systems seeking to implement Stratified Navigation techniques.

Our team conducted an in-depth analysis of Nereid, one of the largest and earliest discovered moons of Neptune. Using the data from Nereid's spectral analysis between 0.45 and 2.45 micrometers, we found that Nereid has characteristics similar to other icy bodies in the solar system. notably, we detected the presence of water ice OH, OH oscillations, and crystal OH features in Nereid's spectrum. We found that these ice components are uniformly distributed across the surface of Nereid. However, we were unable to determine the relative abundance of these water ice components, and any such abundance we calculated would not be accurate due to limitations in our data. In addition, we conducted comparisons of Nereid's spectral features with other Neptunian moons and discovered that Nereid has more water ice than any other Neptune moon. Finally, we calculated that Nereid is composed primarily of water ice, and that Tholen categories can't accurately describe the mineralogical composition of active outer solar system bodies.

We examine the point sets defined by equations of the form $f(\mathbf{x}) = 0$, where $f$ is a quadratic form, in spaces $\mathbb{T}_n(\mathbf{k})$ and $\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{k})$ representing affine and projective spaces over rings $\mathbf{k}$ consisting of lower triangular matrices of size $3 \times 3$ and entries from a field $\mathbf{k}$. Our investigation reveals various properties and relationships of these quadratic point sets.

We employ the use of a tree-formulated quasi metric to demonstrate an enhanced version of a previously formulated metric by Pawlikowski based on the Rayitchou-Tukey sequence theory. The established improvement presents a more precise and fundamental concept than what was originally proposed by Pawlikowski. Furthermore, the new framework is shown to be a special instance of a broader principle suggested by Pawlikowski.

In the context of Bayesian dynamic treatment analysis, where treatment decisions and unobserved factors evolve over discrete time periods, we enhance the implicit pessimism concept for uncertain situations. Our approach utilizes a Bayesian learning strategy, where the prior belief about unobserved variables changes based on observed information up to the current time point, thereby forming time-specific posterior priors. These adjusted priors are then employed to formulate a Bayesian dynamic treatment strategy, where each decision is conditioned on the current time-sensitive posterior/priors. When the current time sensitivity is low, this strategy aligns with standard Bayesian decision-making under uncertainty. When it is high, this strategy mimics the pessimism principle. We derive a general Bayesian formula, applicable to any loss function, that calculates the minimum achievable cost loss by leveraging time sensitivity. We apply this result to a Bayesian linear model with a quadratic loss function to provide empirical evidence, showcasing how pessimism and Bayesian strategies can lead to distinct cost losses. Our study highlights the relationship between cost loss and time sensitivity and explores a case where the time sensitivity remains constant over time.

Dualities in category theory serve as valuable tools for creating equivalences, 
which subsequently facilitate comparisons between invariants, 
resulting in the discovery of invariants' intrinsic properties. This memo highlights 
various reunifications of previously established dualities through the lens of homological methods, 
which enable the reunification of distinct interpretations of invariants, 
 thereby demonstrating their inevitable characteristics. Moreover, it outlines
  additional dualities with applications in invariant calculation that can be
  explored further. To achieve these aims, distinct interpretations of homological invariants, a perspective from a prior study that categorizes invariants as functors, and the framework for functors on 1-categories and 2-categories are established.

A model is devised to examine the potential of quantum entanglement and contextuality by integrating complex numbers with $E_8$'s structure, specifically through the concept of "complex $E_8$ spinors". A total of 246 complex numbers, each associated with a specific direction in a 240-dimensional space, are assigned a probability of 1/246 in this model, with that probability representing a measurement of the corresponding $E_8$ root vector in a complex $E_8$ element, known as $\chi$. It becomes evident that strong quantum entanglement and contextuality are both present in this model, with contextuality exhibiting an even stronger level than that found in the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger experiment. Furthermore, the model demonstrates that any given observer can only select 80 distinct measurement devices, with 120 root vectors becoming inaccessible to that observer.

We investigate two-dimensional superconducting systems featuring an almost-flat band of a specific symmetry with a fully occupied opposite symmetry band, categorizing it as a topological flat band system based on its wave function characteristics. This system gives rise to a uniquely labeled order parameter with distinct quantum numbers, which we define as the topological ($T$) and symmetry ($S$) components. Due to the system's topological properties, $T$ can only assume binary values. Introducing a pairing potential, which we denote as $\Delta$, primarily affects the $\Delta S$ component but is constrained to be non-zero, thereby restricting the value of $T$ to zero and resulting in a separation between the ground state values of $T$. This situation is analyzed through the application of Berry connection, which leads to a body-centered momentum dependence of $\Delta S$. Consequently, this momentum dependence of $\Delta S$ is found to be directly associated with the emergence of multi-partite entanglement within the system. Moreover, multi-partite correlations within the system are quantified to assess the multi-partite correlation order within the system. Importantly, both the momentum dependence of $\Delta S$ and multi-partite correlation order within the system are found to be universally determined by wave function properties. This finding suggests that multi-body ordered states with high correlation orders are naturally produced within systems exhibiting topological characteristics, which is a significant aspect within the context of topological quantum matter.

In 1922, P. Polya established a cornerstone result stating that any two compact groups, $H_1$ and $H_2$, with the same collection of irreducible characters are indistinguishable in structure and equivalence in class. This raised the question of whether this result holds for linked groups. A type of linked relationship between groups was introduced in this study, and we have shown that the diameter of their associated linked coordinate sets must be the same. Furthermore, we've found that the Frolikov dimension of these groups needs to be the same as a result of this relationship. Building on this, the main result of this paper asserts that two locally compact, Abelian groups, $H_1$ and $H_2$, where the first has a countably generated dual group, are interchangeable in class when they have similar sets of one-dimensional unitary representations. Additionally, we have determined that the $\sigma$-compactness of these groups should also be the same for this class equivalence to hold. Furthermore, it has been proven that the set of one-dimensional unitary representations of countably generated dual groups provides sufficient information about their duality structure, and also their Malliard measurable space configurations. These findings have further revealed that this set can also give insights into the continuous spectrum and topological properties of these groups.

When analyzing presence-absence data from collections of items, 
researchers have discovered that various types of objects exist in specific locations, 
indicated by their presence. This study investigates different clustering techniques 
for categorizing such binary data into distinct groups, focusing on scenarios where 
data follows a sparse binary pattern, such as in biological or textual datasets. 
However, existing evaluation methods are either impractical or inadequate in this context. 
This research develops novel evaluation metrics tailored to sparse-data models and conducts 
an empirical comparison of various clustering algorithms using those metrics under controlled 
experimental conditions. The analysis compares multiple methods, including the adaptation of 
existing algorithms to sparse-data settings and uses high-dimensional features combined with 
traditional clustering tools. The results show that diverse clustering algorithms perform well 
and highlight nuances in their strengths under different circumstances.

Despite the existence of various methods for identifying prominent items in visual data from both medical and commercial sources, they often struggle with real-world complexity and fail to effectively address the challenges of extracting information from existing medical data. A novel approach to salient item identification in 2D RGB and RGB-D images is introduced, which outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods through a blend of contextual cues, boundary enhancement, and multi-scale feature extraction techniques. A comprehensive evaluation of this method is conducted on multiple datasets without any adjustments and positive results are observed at both empirical and theoretical levels. A thorough analysis of its applicability is provided in cases involving medical imaging and marketing data. The method demonstrates robustness and consistency in handling challenging inputs due to its direct addressing of contextual cues, boundary enhancement, and multi-scale features. Notably, it achieves impressive outcomes, including state-of-the-art performance in 2D medical data and a successful deployment in extracting data from medical images and a high-converting e-commerce website, where it achieves an exceptional average conversion rate of 10.35%.

The UM-IU@LING system is an entry for the SemEval-2019.16 Offensive Language Identification competition, focusing on subtasks A and B that categorize tweets into 'offensive towards the user' and 'offensive' respectively. Our approach involves ensembling a support vector machine with BERT, a pre-trained language model, on various text representations. Notably, we are one of two UM-IU systems participating in the competition.

A real number $x$ has a finite binary expansion if it can be written as an infinite series $0.d_1d_2\dots$. This expansion can be broken down into blocks, with a focus on a specific type of block known $\beta$-palindromic, where the sequence of elements within each block reads the same forwards and backwards. Only real numbers between $-1$ and $1$ can have such blocks. We examine the proportion of all possible blocks that are $\beta$-palindromic, or have an equivalent reverse, relative to the total number of possible blocks of any given length. We also provide a comparative analysis of the frequencies of these palindromic blocks versus those blocks that are not equivalent to any other block of the same length.

Non-X-ray computed tomography (CT) techniques have garnered interest due to their enhanced safety for live subjects; however, they often suffer from limited spatial resolution and extremely poor signal quality resulting from inferior detection capabilities of non-X-ray detectors. To address these shortcomings, we propose a novel variational reconstruction model that simultaneously optimizes material decomposition, breakdown, and binary segmentation while considering data noise. This unified model streamlines complex reconstruction problems into a single, cohesive entity. We employ the alternating direction method of multipliers to solve the single optimization problem efficiently. Moreover, our approach reveals that traditional multi-energy CT methods can be viewed as a special case, thus facilitating parameter selection. Three-dimensional CT scans from both synthetic and real data demonstrate that our method yields superior image quality and breakdown results compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Recent advancements in Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) have largely relied on neural network-based approaches that demand substantial computational resources. However, training such models from scratch is impractical for many researchers due to their resource requirements. To address this limitation, we introduce single-shot data creation methods that allow for the efficient generation of realistic handwritten text images. These models produce images based on a straightforward input of word characters and a provided sample image. To achieve greater realism, we incorporate complex writing processes and overlay the generated images with realistic background and texture effects. Moreover, we develop a strategy to introduce realistic variations in character orientations. To test the effectiveness of our model under resource-constrained conditions, we conduct handwritten text recognition experiments with limited resource budgets, evaluating the performance on the ITC-HST and ITCHST datasets.
